  ran under the room lock (RFC §10.1 step 9a, RMK-930). A delete committed
  during an edit's hooks (a hook's `send_event()`, which commits ahead of
  the edit) was undone by the edit, which wrote the target's old metadata
  back with its new content; the edit is now refused
  `target_event_not_found`, and nothing of it, its hooks' injected events
  included, is stored.

- An accepted edit or delete reaches no one who could not see its target
  (RFC §10.3 state updates 4 and 5, RMK-930): its visibility, narrowed by its
  source binding's, is narrowed again to its target's, and an injected
  change reaches those of its targets that could see the target. A
  correction of a message only an advisor saw reached the customer. The
  change is also delivered with its target as its commit left it: the
  history handed with an edit held the target's old content, and with a
  delete the target not yet marked deleted.

- A hook's modify keeps what step 8a checked of an edit or a delete (RFC
  §9.4, §10.3, RMK-930): its target, and now its `edit_source` or
  `delete_type` and its kind of content. A hook could turn a sender's edit
  into a system one, a SENDER delete into an ADMIN one, or hide a change
  the step never checked: a message rewritten as an `EditContent`, an
  edit's new content made a delete, a composite with a change among its
  parts. Such a replacement leaves the original's content; an edit's new
  content and a delete's reason as the hook rewrote them still stand, and
  an edit rewritten as text still says that text.

- An edit or a delete targets an event of its room that is not BLOCKED, not
  deleted and not itself an edit or a delete (RFC §10.3 rule 2, RMK-930);
  only existence and the room were checked. A refused message could be
  edited, a deleted one edited or deleted again, and a change changed. Each
  is now refused `target_event_not_found`. An edited message may still be
  edited again, and a retried delete that carries its idempotency key is
  still answered as the first (§13.4).

- An event is an edit only when its type is EDIT and its content an
  `EditContent`, a delete only when DELETE and `DeleteContent` (RFC §10.3
  rule 1, RMK-930). Step 8a ran only when the two agreed, while a channel
  applies a change natively by its content alone: a MESSAGE carrying an
  `EditContent`, or a composite with an edit among its parts, reached
  edit-capable channels with no target, author or authority checked. A type
  and a content that disagree, and a change held anywhere else (a
  composite's part, an edit's new content), are now refused
  `target_event_not_found`, nothing stored.

- `LlamaCppAIProvider`'s start timeout names the budget it was given
  (RMK-922). The message rounded `startup_timeout` to the second, so a
  budget under one second read "not ready after 0s"; it now prints the
  configured value ("not ready after 0.1s", "not ready after 120s").

- An intelligence channel the event solicits that is not registered is
  reported failed (RFC §8.2, §10.2 step 3, RMK-930). Its binding outlives
  the channel, and the router skipped it with a warning: the turn the
  event owed it was never taken and nothing said so. It is now reported
  `delivery_failed` with the error `channel_not_registered`, counted in
  `broadcast_partial_failure`, and the result's `delivery_results` names it
  `failed` (code `channel_not_registered`, not retryable); it ran no turn,
  so `ON_ERROR` does not fire, and it stays in `unavailable_targets`. An
  agent the event does not solicit, and a transport, whose client may be
  connected to another process, are still skipped without a report.

### Security

- A routed message's room is checked again under the room lock, not only its
  binding (RFC §10.1 step 2, §10.4, RMK-930). Someone heard on the channel, or
  added on it as a member, between the router's read and the lock no longer
  lets the sender be recorded on a binding that named no one: the agent's
  answers to that person would have gone to the sender. The check is the
  default router's own step 3, whichever router chose the room, and a message
  with no address takes it as any sender's does; only the framework's own
  sender (`system`) is spared it. A room closed or archived by then, a paused
  one that is not the sender's conversation (its binding names them, a
  participant they are was reached through the channel, or the binding is
  `group`), and a binding naming another correspondent, by its participant or
  else its recipient, leave the room as it was: the message is routed once
  more, its identity not read again, and a second answer that is not the
  message's, like none, gives it a new room. A routed room that does not bind
  the channel is attached under that lock, after the check, so one that is no
  longer the message's gets no binding. Before, a room closed meanwhile
  refused the message `room_closed`, the second answer was kept whatever it
  was, and a stranger routed to a binding holding only a recipient wrote that
  recipient on it. A member of the room reached through the channel no longer
  lands in it when its binding names someone else: the room answers that
  person's address. A message routed to an existing room now takes its lock
  once before step 3, whether or not anything is recorded.

- **BREAKING — an id names its participant only on a channel the room reached
  them through** (RMK-915, RFC §5.5). The label a transcript gave a sender
  already followed this rule; what the sender was granted did not. So a sender
  whose id equalled a participant reached through another channel only got
  that participant's role and its tool policy override, their administrative
  authority for an ADMIN delete, their authorship for editing or deleting
  their messages, the identification that skips identity resolution, and their
  verification label: a message on `web` carrying the id of an identity
  verified through SMS was stamped `verified` and released to the agent. All
  of these now read one lookup. An identity's id names its person on a channel
  one of their records was reached through (the identity pipeline records the
  channel it resolved them on), no longer on any. Three more readings follow
  the rule:
  - `current_tool_actor_id()` is `None` when the sender's id is a
    participant's reached through other channels only: a handler resolving it
    would otherwise act for that participant;
  - inbound routing (RFC §10.4 step 1) finds a room through a participant
    record only when that participant joined it through the message's channel:
    a sender borrowing the id of a room's owner on another channel no longer
    lands in that room nor claims its binding, which would have sent the
    room's replies to them;
  - a pending sender whose id names a record reached through other channels
    only gets a record of its own, one per sender and channel, and writes
    under its id, instead of adopting the other record.
  Migrate: a host that relied on two transports sharing ids links the person
  explicitly, with `add_member` (or `join`, `ensure_participant`) on each
  channel, or through the identity pipeline.

- `update_event()` and `delete_event()` take the organization the caller
  acts for (RFC §17.2, §10.3, RMK-930). A tenant's host could rewrite or
  delete an event of another tenant's room, and the call applied that
  room's due timers. `update_event(room_id, event_id, ...,
  organization_id=None)` and `delete_event(room_id, event_id, *,
  cascade_replies=True, organization_id=None)` act on another
  organization's room as on a missing one (`None`, an empty list): nothing
  written, its due timers included, no hook. Unset, the call is unscoped,
  as the kit's other calls.

- A delivery status is dispatched within the organization the caller acts
  for (RFC §17.2, RMK-930). `process_webhook(meta, channel_id,
  organization_id=...)` scoped only an inbound message: a status that named no
  room was routed among every organization's rooms, so on a channel shared by
  two tenants one tenant's status reached the other's newer room, its context
  and its `ON_DELIVERY_STATUS` hooks. `process_delivery_status(status, *,
  organization_id=None)` takes the organization (unset: unscoped, as the
  other kit calls); its routing reads that organization's rooms only, a room
  the status names that is another organization's is not dispatched in, and
  `process_webhook()` passes its organization to it.

## [0.107.0] — 2026-10-21

### Added

- A turn that an executor runs in another process shows as one trace with
  the owner's spans (RMK-836, RFC §10.6.9): its request carries the W3C trace
  context of the span it runs under (`traceparent`, `tracestate`, as the
  application's OpenTelemetry propagator writes them), and the executor's
  spans continue it. Give the executor's process an `OpenTelemetryProvider`
  (`TurnExecutor(telemetry=...)`). The request carried the span's id only,
  which another process cannot resolve: its `OpenTelemetryProvider` logged
  "Parent span not found" and started a new trace. The default propagator
  also carries the ambient `baggage` (`OTEL_PROPAGATORS=tracecontext` keeps
  it in its process), and the executor follows the owner's sampling decision.
  `TelemetryProvider` gains `inject_context(span_id)` and
  `extract_context(carrier)`, optional (`{}` and `None` by default), and
  `TurnClient` a `telemetry=` the kit sets. An `OpenTelemetryProvider` span
  started with an explicit parent now nests under it rather than under the
  context an ancestor propagated: a turn's generation is its broadcast's
  child, where it was the inbound pipeline's, and its tool calls the
  generation's.

- `InboundMessage.delivery_key` and `kit.cancel_delivery(key)` (RMK-860, RFC
  §10.1): a caller names a message's delivery by a key of its own and cancels
  it from anywhere in the process, without its handle, so an agent's tool can
  pass a task id along as text. It answers how many deliveries in flight the
  key named and cancelled, returns at once (a sync hook or a tool handler
  included), and each call's caller reads the cancelled end on its result.
  Several messages may share a key; the key is never stored and grants
  nothing, and `organization_id=` keeps a cancellation to the caller's rooms
  (RFC §17.2), so two tenants that chose the same key never cancel each
  other's. Two tasks handed to one agent in one room can now be stopped one at
  a time, where a room's Stop cut the running one and let the waiting one
  start. `examples/cancel_delivery_by_key.py` runs it.

- Phonon text-to-speech, Gradium's small local models (RMK-867,
  `pip install roomkit[phonon]`). `PhononTTSProvider` runs the 31M and 40M
  Phonon models (English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese) in the process
  through their Rust runtime, `ptts`, on the CPU with no torch: about ten
  times faster than real time on two threads, 40–110 ms to the first chunk,
  streamed as 24 kHz PCM. It loads the runtime's default model, Phonon 31m
  English, unless `PhononTTSConfig.model` names another (`hf://` or a local
  checkpoint), takes a catalog voice by name or id or a Gradium Studio voice
  file, fetches the default voice at `warmup()`, and lists the catalog. A
  barge-in stops the runtime's workers in about 60 ms, and replies stream
  side by side from one loaded model. `examples/voice_local_phonon.py` runs a
  local French assistant on it.

- Voxtral 3 speech, Mistral's transcription and TTS (RMK-884,
  `pip install roomkit[mistral-voice]`), so a voice agent runs on Mistral end
  to end beside `MistralAIProvider`. `VoxtralSTTProvider` transcribes a clip
  on Voxtral Mini or Small Transcribe 3 (PCM, a `data:` URI, or an http(s) URL
  Mistral fetches) and streams on Voxtral Mini Transcribe Realtime 3 with the
  model's own turn detection: each turn is a final and its start a speech
  start, in continuous mode, or one final per utterance behind a VAD with
  `turn_detection=None`. A turn's last words arrive up to a streaming delay
  after the model ends it, even after the next turn has started (measured), so
  its final waits that delay plus 100 ms (`final_wait_ms`). The provider
  validates the streaming delay (80–1200 ms or 2400) and the turn thresholds
  before connecting; `VoxtralTurnDetection.aggressive()` is Mistral's faster
  preset (the final about 0.7 s after speech at a 240 ms delay, 1.7 s with the
  defaults). `VoxtralTTSProvider` streams Voxtral Speech 3 as 24 kHz 16-bit
  PCM, converted from the float samples the service sends, and lists every
  voice the workspace can use; its offline catalog holds the 36 Voxtral 3
  presets, four of them French. `examples/voice_voxtral.py` runs the agent.

- `STTProvider.keeps_stream_across_turns` (RMK-887, RFC §12.2): a provider
  whose model cuts the turns within one stream says so, and a `VoiceChannel`
  in continuous mode keeps its stream open across turns, as it does for a
  diarizing provider, instead of reconnecting after each final. Its finals
  reach the room one at a time in the order they were said, the reply to one
  never holding back the next. `VoxtralSTTProvider` claims it whenever turn
  detection is on.

- Speaker labels on Voxtral (RMK-885): `VoxtralSTTConfig(diarize=True,
  turn_detection=None)` makes `VoxtralSTTProvider` report
  `supports_diarization`, and every final name its speaker in `segments`
  (RFC §12.2.3), Mistral's `speaker_1` arriving as `"1"`. A file comes back
  with one segment per run of a speaker and its times. Live, the service
  cannot label speakers and detect turns in one session (the config refuses
  both), so a turn ends when another voice starts or after a pause without
  new words (`diarized_pause_ms`, 1.5 s: one person's words came up to 2 s
  apart, a new speaker's 1.5 s after the last, measured); a `VoiceChannel`
  carries the labels in continuous mode on one session.
  `speaker_references` names known voices live from 3 to 15 s clips, at most
  8; the model's matching is partial (a voice came back under its name, then
  as "3", in one measured session), and the file endpoint ignored them.
  `examples/voice_voxtral_diarization.py` labels the voices around one
  microphone.

### Changed

- **BREAKING — the kit's own executor alone takes the turns of the agents the
  kit holds live** (RMK-837, RFC §10.6.7), their channel calls and the
  events a discussion hands their memories included, whatever other executor
  is served on the kit's turn backend. An executor a host served there first,
  without `hosts=` or naming the agent, used to take them: its own copy of the
  agent answered, the hooks registered on the kit (a `BEFORE_TOOL_USE` guard
  among them) never fired, and a turn its factory had no channel for failed.
  Now the agent the kit holds answers, its kit hooks fire, and a turn the
  kit's executor does not take (a room hook enabled for the room that it does
  not define) fails with `no_executor` rather than moving to another
  executor. To run an agent on a host's executor, register its
  `ChannelDeclaration` on the kit instead of the agent; `RoomOwner.executor`
  is how a backend learns which executor is the owner's.

- Cancelling a delivery stops its turns, not its delivery (RMK-860, RFC §10.1):
  `result.delivery.cancel()`, a cancelled awaited `process_inbound()` /
  `send_event()` / `regenerate_response()` and `kit.cancel_delivery()` cancel
  the intelligence targets' turns and the reading of their streams, and a turn
  not started yet never starts; the message is still delivered to the room's
  other channels and its AFTER_BROADCAST hooks fire, an event a hook injected
  for it starting no turn either. The cancel joins the turns' work only, never
  a transport still delivering. A message cancelled while it waited in the
  room's lane used to be stored without reaching any transport or firing its
  hooks, so a host's live view and audit missed it.

- A turn no longer scans the history the last turn read for a copy of the
  turn's notes' header (RMK-844, RFC §6.4): a text seen to hold none is
  remembered by a digest and returned as it is, as a text seen to hold no copy
  of the runtime's other marks already was. The header's scan ran over every
  message of the history on every turn, about 60 µs per KB: a turn that
  streams 2000 deltas over a history of 50 stored answers of 8 KB goes from
  18 ms to 9.3 ms of CPU. A text new to the turn is scanned as before, and one
  holding a copy is replaced every time. A run of consecutive user messages
  the runtime did not label is still scanned whole, the new input with it, for
  a copy split over them.

- What a turn's request costs, carrying the room's recent history with each
  event's full metadata, is documented and kept as it is (RMK-843): with 51
  events, about 0.4 ms of CPU per turn for plain messages and about 1 ms when
  each stored answer carries some 7 KB of metadata. Data that heavy, wanted on
  every message, is better kept in a store of the application's own and
  referenced from the event by an id.

### Fixed

- A turn a person starts soon after the previous one reaches the room whole
  with Voxtral (RMK-887). On a stream per turn, its first words went to the
  stream the channel was closing and came back as a turn of their own ("What
  is the capital of Italy?", "Answer", "in one word."); the stream is now
  kept. A turn that starts while the last one waits for its last words also
  closes that one sooner, 0.95 of the streaming delay after its end: its last
  words came up to 0.9 of the delay after the end (0.43 s at 480 ms,
  measured), and the new turn's first word comes no sooner than a delay after
  it, where the plain wait (the delay plus 100 ms) had joined that word to
  the last turn.

- A `HandoffHandler` serving a realtime voice channel refuses an agent that
  is not an `Agent` (one the kit holds by its declaration alone, or another
  intelligence channel) with a `ValueError` naming it (RMK-831, RFC §19.5,
  §19.6): the channel's sessions run each agent's own prompt, which only an
  `Agent` carries. It refuses one when given it while `event_channel_id`
  names a realtime channel the kit holds, and `set_language()` refuses one
  before writing the room's language when the channel it reconfigures
  (`channel_id=` or `event_channel_id`) is realtime, whoever put the agent in
  its `agents`; `set_language()` raised `AttributeError` at the first
  language change. An object that is not an `Agent` but carries
  `system_prompt` and `build_identity_block`, which `set_language()` took,
  is refused too. `ConversationPipeline` refuses such agents by the same
  rule. A handler serving no realtime channel (Swarm's, Pipeline's, a text
  one) still takes declared agents.

- `cancel_task` answers a task of the room it may not cancel as still running,
  and why (RMK-829, RFC §23.4): an inline delegation runs inside the turn that
  asked for it and ends with it, and a task a strategy runs unposted, inline
  or in the background, is the strategy's. It answered `unknown` ("No task …
  here"), so an agent shown the task running by `task_status` was told it did
  not exist. Whether a task the bus lists running is the room's is the kit's
  own record of the tasks it runs for each room, never the status bus: another
  room's task, an id the kit never ran, or a task another kit runs for the
  room on a bus both share, still answers `unknown`; a task the bus lists
  ended is answered as it lists it, as `task_status` does. A task of the room
  that ended answers that it had ended, with its status, while the bus still
  shows it running (an inline task from its completion's start, before its
  hooks; a background one once its runner hands its end over; the kit keeps
  the latest 1024 ended, all rooms together), where it answered `unknown`. A
  task whose pending entry left the bus's window, its progress alone left, is
  listed running as the turn's notes read it, and `cancel_task` cancels it,
  where it answered that it had ended. The console's `/cancel` says why an
  inline run is still running, in the tool's words, where it said it had
  ended, says a task its line lists ended had ended, and cancels only a task
  the kit runs for its room: a line of the room naming another room's task
  cancelled that task.

- A Redis turn backend whose Redis goes silent without closing a connection
  (a NAT or a load balancer forgot it) keeps the process among the living
  (RMK-859, RFC §10.6.8). Its connections set no timeout, so with a redis-py
  before 8.0, which the `redis` extra admitted, the beat, the inbox's read and
  an outbox write waited until TCP gave up, about 15 minutes: the other
  processes took this one for lost and cut its turns. Each connection the
  backend opens now gives up a call after half of `heartbeat_timeout` (5 s by
  default; the inbox's blocking read waits the time Redis holds it more, a
  second at most and never over `heartbeat_interval`), and the beat or the
  read it cut is tried again at once on a new connection: while
  `heartbeat_interval` stays under half of `heartbeat_timeout` (the defaults:
  2 s and 10 s), that try lands inside the silence bound. A turn's message
  whose write was cut fails its turn. A read of the processes alive that its
  connection cut counts from its start, as one that hung, so a Redis that
  froze leaves the others unread about `heartbeat_timeout` later. A client
  passed as `client=` keeps its own settings, and no pool is built beside it.
  The extra now needs `redis>=5.0.2`: 5.0.1's connection pool blocked every
  caller on a silent Redis.

- A turn already over whose `end` never came (its drain past
  `cancel_timeout`, its executor lost) stays incomplete when its owner closes
  (RMK-832, RFC §10.1, §10.6.8). The owner's close gave up every turn it held,
  over or not, so a cascade still cleaning up when the kit closed reported such
  a turn's cleanup done, where incomplete drainage MUST be reported. The close
  gives up only the turns still open.

- A discussion asks its `done` before it gives a turn or dispatches a
  message, one queued while it looked at the queue included (RMK-835, RFC
  §19.7.5 rule 15). Its driver reads the queue off the room lock and asked
  `done` only when that read held something, then planned from the queue read
  again under the lock: a message queued in between reached the dispatch
  policy, or took its turn, with `done` never asked, so a discussion `done`
  said was over still gave it, and a `done` that uninstalls the discussion
  never ran. Across Redis, where handing a message to the agents' memories
  delays its routing into the queue, a pass begun meanwhile missed it every
  time. Now such a pass plans nothing and the next one asks `done` first.

- A delegated task keeps the answer of the agent it was delegated to, and
  fails on that agent's own cut only, whatever other agent shares the child
  room (RMK-834, RFC §23.3 step 6), on the shared-transport path and the trace
  path alike. It kept the first responder's answer in the order their turns
  returned, so a helper shared into the room that answered sooner gave the
  task its answer, or hid that the worker was cut, and across Redis the order
  followed the latency; without a shared transport, a helper cut short failed
  the task with the helper's narration and end, the worker's answer lost, and
  a worker owing its result was not re-prompted. A worker that gave no answer
  while a shared helper did now fails the task where it completed with the
  helper's answer. A helper whose turn fails with an error still fails the
  task, as before. The RFC now says that a message's own responses are read
  in the order their turns return them (§10.1 step 14).

- A turn's executor cancels the turn's running work once (RMK-860, RFC
  §10.6.8): a stream close that reached it while a cut's cleanup ran, or a cut
  that reached it while a close's cleanup ran, cancelled that cleanup again, so
  a channel's stream finalizer awaiting something (a provider closing its
  connection) was interrupted halfway and the turn's end was written before it
  had finished.

- Mistral Large 4 (`mistral-large-4-0`, `mistral-large-4`) carries its list
  price in the Mistral catalog, $1.36 / $4.18 per million, cache reads $0.14
  (verified 2026-10-21 on its model card). Its launch price, half of that,
  ended, so the catalog's $0.68 / $2.09 / $0.07 since 0.96.0 halved every
  cost a host computed for it.

## [0.106.0] — 2026-10-19

### Added

- `benchmarks/rtp/` measures how many G.711 calls one core carries on the RTP
  media path, the work a SIP call does before any voice pipeline stage
  (RMK-794). One Rust generator drives each system under test: aiortp (one
  `RTPSession` per call, optionally with adaptive playout or uvloop) and a
  native Rust echo with a media server's hot path (one socket per call, or one
  shared socket per thread with `recvmmsg`/`sendmmsg`). Loss, round-trip time
  and gaps come from timestamps carried in the echoed audio, never from the
  server's own counters, and `--find-max` searches for the largest call count
  that passes. A point disturbed by other processes or by a struggling
  generator is retried, never blamed on the system under test. On one
  performance core over loopback: aiortp 0.7.0 carries 950 calls (10.4 µs per
  packet) and the native engine 5250 to 8250 (1.7 to 1.07 µs). The suite lives
  outside the installed package and needs a Rust toolchain; Linux only.
  `benchmarks/voice` measures what RoomKit adds per frame past RTP.

- `benchmarks/voice/` measures the CPU RoomKit spends per inbound 20 ms voice
  frame once a transport has decoded it (RMK-796): `python -m benchmarks.voice`
  feeds N sessions, one room each, through a mock backend's audio callback,
  with the energy VAD or none and a batch or streaming mock STT, and reports
  µs per frame, calls per core for that layer and the STT requests, so two
  runs can be checked to have detected the same turns. RTP, codecs and models
  are excluded. `--dsn` runs the same turns with the rooms in Postgres
  (RMK-797), and a run waits for the process to stop spending CPU before it
  closes the kit, so turns still queued for the store's connections are
  measured rather than dropped.

- `RedisTurnBackend` (RMK-813, RFC §10.6.7 to §10.6.9, `pip install
  roomkit[redis]`): an agent's turns run on an executor in another process
  or on another machine, while the kit keeps the room. One backend per
  process on a shared Redis and a shared store: `RoomKit(store=...,
  turn_backend=RedisTurnBackend(url))` on the owner, `await
  backend.serve(TurnExecutor(build, hosts={"meteo"}, store=...))` on the
  executor. Each process reads one inbox stream and writes to the others in
  order, one writer per destination; each beats from a thread of its own, on
  Redis's clock, declaring its executors again at every beat. A turn counts
  alive while its executor beats and its process still runs it: a turn busy
  with its CPU is slow, never lost; a killed executor, or a write Redis
  refuses, fails the turn within `heartbeat_timeout`. A request reaches one
  executor at most: its process acknowledges it, a closed executor's refusal
  places it again, and one a client writes twice (a pipeline it retries) is
  taken once. A process that closes stops declaring its executors (nothing
  new is placed there) and beats on while it answers what it was applying
  (within `cancel_timeout`) and writes what it queued (a turn's end, within
  `cancel_timeout` again), refusing at once what reaches it meanwhile (a
  turn is placed on another executor); then it withdraws.
  A room's turns stay on the executor that holds its state
  while it lives (the holder is shared by every owner process), else go to
  one that takes them; a turn no executor declares fails at once with
  `no_executor`. Channel controls are applied on the executor before the
  owner goes on. The agents the kit registers live stay in its process. Work
  a turn began reaches the owner that submitted it, while that owner lives.
  `client=` needs `url=` too (the beat connects with it). Needs Redis 6.2
  or later. Redis is the trust boundary (ACL, TLS). Example:
  `examples/turns_redis.py`; guide: Agent Turns in Another Process (Redis).

- `TurnExecutor(hosts=...)` also takes the set of channel ids the executor
  runs (RMK-813, RFC §10.6.7); only an executor declared with a set takes
  turns from other processes, one given a predicate those of its own
  process. `TurnBackend.timeouts` gives the kit and its own executor the
  backend's bounds, and `TurnLink.beat_heard()` lets a backend count a beat
  its executor makes outside the turn's messages (RFC §10.6.8). A backend
  marks a request or a channel call handed (`hand_over()`) as it gives it to
  an executor, before any wait on its answer: one that failed before stays
  out of the room's previous turn, and one handed stays in it, a cancel or a
  timeout included (RFC §10.6.2).

- Strategies and the owner's tools take an agent the kit holds by its
  declaration alone, named by its channel id (RMK-826, RFC §10.6.2):
  `Supervisor`, `Loop`, `Swarm`, `Pipeline`, `Discussion`,
  `ConversationRouter.install`, `ConversationPipeline.install`,
  `setup_handoff`, `setup_delegation`, `kit.setup_background` and
  `kit.setup_task_tools` take `Agent | str`. An id is read on the kit at the
  install, its tools kept beside its declaration and listed in its turns on
  the executor that builds it; an id the kit does not hold raises
  `ChannelNotRegisteredError`. `AgentIdentity` carries `purpose` and `voice`,
  and a `DeclaredChannel` reads its identity as an `Agent` does (`name`,
  `role`, `description`, `scope`, `greeting`, `language`, `purpose`, `voice`,
  `thinks_while_listening`). A realtime `ConversationPipeline` takes live
  agents only. A Discussion addresses an agent named by an id that is no
  handle by its declared name, as a live one by its own. A declaration says
  whether its turns take the owner's tools (`takes_owner_tools`, true by
  default; an `ACPChannel`'s says false): the owner refuses to set a tool up
  for one that does not (`ValueError`), live or declared, and reads such a
  worker's delegated result as its text. `unregister_channel` drops the
  tools set up for the channel. Example: `examples/declared_supervisor.py`.

- The kit holds an agent by its declaration alone (RMK-822, RFC §10.6.2).
  `kit.register_channel(ChannelDeclaration(channel_id=..., identity=
  AgentIdentity(...), capabilities=..., recent_events_window=...))` registers
  an intelligence channel with no object of it in the kit's process: the kit
  holds a `DeclaredChannel` under its id, which a binding, routing,
  `delegate`, `start_task`, `send_greeting` and auto-greet read as they read
  a live agent. Its turns run on an executor whose host builds it; the kit's
  own executor never builds it, so with none they fail at once with
  `no_executor`. A field left out reads as an `AIChannel` built with its
  defaults (text, rich and media capabilities, a 50-event history).
  `Channel.declaration()` gives any channel's declaration (`Agent` its
  identity, `AIChannel` whether it thinks while listening), and registering
  it reads on the kit as registering the agent does. A declaration that is
  not an intelligence channel's, a binding of one with another category, and
  a strategy given a live agent whose id the kit holds by declaration are
  refused with `ValueError`, the strategy registering none of the agents it
  was given; an intelligence channel whose own declaration is invalid (an
  empty id, a negative window) is refused before it is registered. Example:
  `examples/declared_agent.py`.

- `RoomKit.setup_task_tools(agent)` (RMK-825, RFC §23.4, §10.6.5): gives an AI
  channel `task_status` and `cancel_task` as tools the room's owner serves,
  wherever the agent's turns run, as `setup_background` gives
  `work_in_background`. `TaskStatusTool(kit)` / `CancelTaskTool(kit)` stay the
  same tools for an agent run in the kit's process.

- An executor wires the channels it runs (RMK-821, RFC §10.6.2, §10.6.6). A
  `TurnExecutor` a host builds (`TurnExecutor(build_channel, store=,
  media_resolver=, attached_media=, telemetry=)`) builds each channel once,
  gives it what the kit gives a channel it registers (the callbacks its loop
  fires `BEFORE_TOOL_USE`, `ON_TOOL_CALL`, `ON_AI_RESPONSE` and the other turn
  triggers through, a realtime backend, its tool-memory reader, the host's
  media readers), fires its own hooks against a room context read from the
  given store, and closes what it built when it closes. The kit's own
  executor is wired by the same code (`kit.turn_executor.wire(channel)` at
  `register_channel`), from the kit. During a turn, what a channel publishes
  on its realtime backend and the framework events its hooks emit cross the
  turn backend as `ephemeral` and `framework_event` frames, which the room's
  owner publishes on its realtime backend and its bus (for the turn's room
  only); outside a turn the kit's executor publishes directly, a host's drops
  them. A room's background tasks and what its cameras last saw are read
  through the turn's host (`TurnHost.room_tasks()`, `TurnHost.room_vision()`),
  being state of the owner's process. `ScoringHook.attach` takes an executor,
  and records through the turn's host while the turn runs. The request
  carries the broadcast span's id (`TurnRequest.trace`), which a turn in a
  context of its own continues on the same telemetry provider; an executor
  in another process (`RedisTurnBackend`) does not know that span, so its
  turns start traces of their own until the request carries a W3C trace
  context (RMK-836). The owner publishes what a turn
  published off the turn's frame reader, in order, so a framework-event
  handler may wait on its turn (answer its input, close the kit), and only
  the framework events the wiring emits, as the turn's room and channel.

- Room hooks on the triggers a turn fires are defined by name on the
  executors and enabled per room on the kit (RMK-821, RFC §10.6.6, §10.6.7):
  `executor.room_hook("audit", HookTrigger.ON_TOOL_CALL)(fn)`,
  `kit.enable_room_hook(room_id, "audit")`, `kit.disable_room_hook(room_id,
  "audit")`. A turn's request names its room's (`TurnRequest.room_hooks`), and
  only an executor that defines every name takes it (one given a turn
  anyway fails it with `no_executor`). Enabling or disabling applies to the
  kit's own executor at once, so realtime voice and conference tool calls in
  the room run the room's hooks too; a turn runs the hooks its request
  named, scoped to the turn, never overwriting the room's set with its copy
  (RMK-821 security review). Defining a name on a trigger again
  replaces it. A turn executor's engine refuses a room hook by callable.

- `RoomKit.channel_call(channel_id, room_id, verb, *, organization_id=None,
  **arguments)` (RMK-812, RFC §10.6.3, §6.4): a per-room verb of a channel
  attached to the room (`ChannelNotFoundError` otherwise), run on the
  executor that holds the room's state for the channel (`ChannelCall`,
  answered by a `ChannelResult`), wherever the channel's turns run. An
  `ACPChannel`'s are
  its session's: `set_config_option` (`config_id`, `value`),
  `close_session`, `session_config` and `config_options`, each answering as
  the method of that name; another verb raises `ValueError`. What the room
  keeps for the channel, when a verb changes it, is stored with the room
  (room metadata `roomkit:channel_state:<channel_id>`) and handed to the
  channel before the room's next turn or channel call, so the values a host
  set on an ACP session are set on the session another executor opens for
  the room; a detach forgets them, even when the executors could not be told.
  A value set on the channel object directly is this process's copy: a
  later channel call stores it only when that call changes the room's
  values (RMK-820). `kit.update_room_metadata` and `kit.create_room` refuse
  that key (`ValueError`), and a turn's `TurnHost.update_room_metadata`
  refuses every `roomkit:` key: what sets up an agent's next session (its
  mode) is written by `channel_call` alone. A channel declares its verbs with
  `Channel.channel_call(room_id, verb, arguments)`, and what belongs to the
  room with `Channel.room_state(room_id)` /
  `Channel.restore_room_state(room_id, state)`. The ACP examples switch
  models through it. `TurnBackend.control(message)` carries it, with
  `RoomAttached` and `RoomDetached`.

- A turn's request names the room's previous turn of its channel
  (`TurnRequest.previous_turn`, `PreviousTurn{turn_id, executor_id}`; RMK-812,
  RFC §10.6.2): the one the owner sent last, recorded as it is sent, a
  channel call included (`ChannelCall.previous_turn`, the call's `call_id`),
  `None` for the first and after the channel was detached from the room. An
  executor whose state for the room was not left by that turn or call drops
  it, by the channel's `on_room_detached`, before the turn or the verb runs:
  the room's turns ran elsewhere since. A record an executor stops keeping
  (past 10 000 rooms) drops the state it vouched for, and a drop that failed
  is tried again on the next turn. The in-memory backend places a room's
  turns and channel calls of a channel on the executor that took the last
  one while it serves and declares the channel, else on the first that
  declares it (RFC §10.6.7).

- `ACPChannel.steer(directive, *, turn_id)` (RMK-812, RFC §21.3): a steering
  `Cancel` reaches the turn it names as `cancel()` would (its session's
  opening stopped, or its prompt cancelled), so the turn ends as its prompt
  returns (its calls stored, `ON_AI_RESPONSE` fired), and answers 1; a turn
  that has not reached the agent yet answers `None`, and its owner cuts it
  as the turn's cancel, as before; another directive answers 0. A
  discussion holding an ACP agent cuts its turn through `kit.steer`, as it
  cuts an AI channel's, wherever the turn runs. An executor awaits a
  channel's `steer()` that is a coroutine, and a `steer()` answering `None`
  is a channel that cannot steer that turn.

- `RoomKit.answer_input(request_id, value)` and
  `RoomKit.reject_input(request_id, reason)` (RMK-811, RFC §10.6.5): a
  human-input request of a turn can be answered on the room owner, wherever
  the turn runs. The executor sends the request (`input_request`) before
  `ON_USER_INPUT_REQUIRED` fires; the owner keeps its record, holds an answer
  that comes before it for 60 s (`TurnTimeouts.input_hold_timeout`), and
  sends it to the executor (`input_answer`), where it settles the request if
  it is still open and says whether it did (`input_taken`): the kit's door
  answers `True` only for an answer the waiting tool reads. The request
  settles where its tool waits, first come first served, as it did: an
  answer the channel's own handler takes (`HumanInputHandler.resolve()`), a
  hook's `BLOCK`, its timeout or a release is never taken back by a later
  answer, and the owner closes its record (`input_closed`). A request still
  open when its turn ends is withdrawn on both sides (its waiter reads it
  released), but a detached one (`HumanInputHandler.create_detached`): its
  creator releases it, and only the owner's record goes with the turn; one
  asked from a task after its turn ended is the handler's alone. Answers the
  kit holds are capped (1024); a request belongs to the turn that opened it.

- `RoomKit.steer(directive, channel_id, *, room_id=None, turn_id=None)`
  (RMK-811, RFC §21.3, §10.6.8): steering through the turn backend. The kit
  resolves the turns of the channel it started and that still run (the turn
  `turn_id`; else the room's, every one for a `Cancel` and the most recent
  for another directive; else the channel's most recent), sends the
  directive as a `steer` on each turn's link, and answers the sum of the
  loops each reached (`steer_result`). The executor applies it to the loops
  of that turn (`AIChannel.steer(..., turn_id=...)`, a loop knowing its
  turn; a `steer()` a channel overrides without `turn_id` is given the
  turn's room instead, and one that raises reaches nothing). A channel
  without steering takes a `Cancel` as its turn's cancel, counted as one: its
  reader reads the end as a closed stream's, each call left open ending
  cancelled. `current_turn_id()` gives a turn's tools and hooks the id
  `turn_id` addresses. The owner now reads a turn's frames as they come, so
  a steering result or a call is heard while nobody reads the turn's stream,
  and a frame it cannot read fails the turn. A discussion cuts an AI agent's
  turn through it.

- `TurnHost` and `current_turn_host()` (RMK-811, RFC §10.6.5): how a host's
  tool, or a hook the executor fires, reaches a room from a turn wherever the
  turn runs. `current_turn_host()` answers inside a call of a host tool during
  a turn and inside a hook its executor fires during it, and `None` anywhere
  else: after the turn ended (a host held past it refuses its verbs), and in
  a tool the room owner serves. Its verbs are `send_event`, `delegate` (in the
  background, its task's id), `wait_task` (the `DelegatedTaskResult`, its
  failure kept in `exception`; `None` past its timeout or for a task the
  room's hosts did not delegate), `post_status`, `update_room_metadata` and
  `add_observation`. Each crosses the turn backend as a `host_call` carrying
  what the turn gave the call (its chain depth, who asked), and runs on the
  owner under it, in a copy of the context of the owner's task reading the
  turn: an event sent into the room from a turn the room's lane reads comes
  back detached, and a delegation inherits the turn's chain depth, so a cycle
  of delegations still ends at `max_chain_depth`. A host acts for its turn's
  room and in that room's organization: a verb naming another room, or
  another organization, raises `ValueError` (a status post's
  `metadata["room_id"]` included, which is the turn's room when it names
  none, RMK-820; a `task` status, which only the framework posts, the room's
  task tools reading it), and an event it sends is at least as deep as the
  turn's response. The owner validates each verb's arguments against its
  record and refuses one the record does not name. A
  verb on its way when its turn ends is answered before the turn ends; an
  error a verb raises is raised in the tool with its class. The owner keeps
  the tasks its hosts delegated while they run, and once ended until 1024
  more ended after them. `DelegatedTaskResult` now lives in
  `roomkit.models.task`; `roomkit.tasks.models` still exports it.

- Every turn of an intelligence channel runs through a turn backend (RMK-809,
  RFC §10.6): `RoomKit(turn_backend=...)`, in memory by default
  (`InMemoryTurnBackend`), with the kit's own `TurnExecutor` reading the
  channels registered on it. The lane submits a `TurnRequest` and reads the
  turn back as the channel's `ChannelOutput`, from serialized messages only,
  the in-memory backend included: the output, a stream whose every read pulls
  one item, the turn's response-metadata record updated as the channel writes
  it, a call's fixed arguments and its end before its end item. The three
  places that call an intelligence channel's `on_event` (a solicited turn and
  the two deliveries of an injected event) go through it; an injected event's
  stream is closed unread, so it never reaches the provider. A turn runs on a
  task of its own, in a copy of the context of the task that submitted it, so
  a tool that calls the kit finds the reentrancy guards it finds today.
  Heartbeats run both ways: a silent executor fails the turn with
  `TurnLinkError` (`executor_lost`, or `no_executor` when none took it), and
  an error of a class outside RoomKit, Python's built-ins and the classes the
  host declares (`error_classes`, below) comes back as `RemoteTurnError`,
  keeping its class name; every error keeps, as a note, where the executor
  raised it. A frame the backend cannot carry (a tool result JSON has no
  form for, an unknown stream item) fails the turn with a
  `TypeError` naming it; a value JSON has no form for in the turn's record,
  or in the room's data its request carries (the room's metadata, an
  event's), crosses as its text. A stream its reader drops, or a cancelled delivery set leaves unread,
  is closed on the executor.

- `ResponseMetadata.writes` counts the writes to a record's keys (RMK-841,
  RFC §10.6.4). A turn's executor reads it before each text or reasoning
  delta and copies the record to compare it only when one of its keys was
  written since; before any other item, at the stream's end and on close it
  compares the record in full. A turn's CPU then no longer grows with the
  size of its record: 2000 deltas with 30 `rag_sources` (about 10 KB) cost
  17 ms, as with no record, against 40 ms with a copy per delta (13 ms in
  0.105.0, which had no turn backend). A change made inside a value the
  record holds (`record["sources"].append(...)`) between two deltas reaches
  the owner before the next item that is no delta, the one ending the
  segment stored with it; a record a channel left a bare dict, past the
  output's validation, is compared before every item.

- `RoomKit(error_classes=...)` and `TurnExecutor(error_classes=...)` (and
  `TurnClient`) name the application's exception classes that cross the turn
  backend as themselves (RMK-838, RFC §10.6.8). Since every turn runs through
  the backend, an error a turn raised reached `InboundResult.error`,
  `ON_ERROR` and its chain of causes as a `RemoteTurnError` without its
  attributes whenever its class was not RoomKit's or a Python built-in: an
  application's classified provider error lost its type, its code and its
  verdicts, and a transport error among its causes (`httpx.ReadTimeout`) its
  type. A declared class and its subclasses come back as themselves, with
  their arguments and the attributes JSON carries, causes included, on the
  kit and on an executor in another process, each reading with its own
  declaration: `RoomKit(error_classes=(AppError, httpx.HTTPError))`. One
  whose message JSON cannot carry (its `__str__` reads an object, a
  `UnicodeDecodeError`'s bytes) comes back as a `RemoteTurnError` that is
  also of its class, its message kept. Any other
  class comes back as a `RemoteTurnError` that keeps its JSON attributes and
  its class's ancestors (`RemoteTurnError.bases`), and that is also an
  instance of the nearest of them the side rebuilds: an application's
  subclass of `ProviderError` still reads as a `ProviderError` (its log line,
  `ON_ERROR`, the resilience layer), and `str()` gives its message unchanged.
  A `RemoteTurnError` that crosses again (a delegated task's failure read by
  `wait_task`) crosses as the error it stands for. An entry that is not an
  `Exception` class raises `TypeError`. A class named on the wire is looked up
  among the names a loaded module defines: it never imports a module nor runs
  a module's code, its `__getattr__` or a lazy loader (a frame naming
  `roomkit.sources:WebSocketSource` imported `roomkit.sources.websocket`).
  Example:
  `examples/turn_error_classes.py`.

- `Discussion(rules=...)` gives each turn the host's rules for how the room
  works, in place of the default (RMK-806, RFC §19.7.5 rule 14). `{handle}` in
  them stands for another agent's `@handle`, an example the agent can follow,
  and `{silent}` for `silent_token`; what the turn knows of the room (its own
  handle, the other agents, the people, what it answers and who asked) stays
  the discussion's. The rules are stored with the discussion's configuration,
  so every process gives its turns with the same, and a configuration stored
  before them reads with the default. Blank rules are refused.

- `RoomKit(attached_media=...)` names the media an application keeps beside a
  message's content (RMK-805, RFC §6.4). An application that stores a message
  as its words, with its files in a record of its own (its metadata, say),
  could give a model its images only by reshaping every message it stores into
  a composite, which every reader of its text then had to learn. The reader,
  `(event) -> Sequence[MediaContent]` (exported as `AttachedMedia`), is asked
  of every event an AI channel reads for a turn, the history it hands its
  memory provider and the event it answers alike; the media it names follow
  the event's own content as the parts of a composite (a text without words
  gives them its place), so an image among them goes as an author's image
  does: resolved by `media_resolver`, under `max_author_images`, refused like
  one, a mention for a model that does not see, and measured and summarized
  by the memory as the turn will send it. The store and every broadcast keep
  the event as stored. The reader names the same media in the same order each
  time it is asked, since an image is known by its event and its place; one
  that raises names none for that event, and an instruction is read as it is.

### Changed

- **BREAKING — an error of the application's own class that a turn raised
  reaches the kit as a `RemoteTurnError` unless the kit declares the class**
  (RMK-809, RMK-838, RFC §10.6.8). Every turn now crosses the turn backend as
  serialized messages, the in-memory default included, and only RoomKit's
  classes, Python's built-ins and the classes named in `error_classes=` come
  back as themselves. `InboundResult.error`, `ON_ERROR` and the error's
  causes carried the class the turn raised (an application's
  `QuotaExceededError`, an `httpx.ReadTimeout` among the causes); they now
  carry a `RemoteTurnError` that keeps the class's name, its JSON attributes
  and the nearest of its ancestors the kit rebuilds, so `except
  QuotaExceededError` no longer catches it while a subclass of
  `ProviderError` still reads as a `ProviderError`. Migration: name the
  classes the application catches or inspects,
  `RoomKit(error_classes=(QuotaExceededError, httpx.HTTPError))`, and the
  same on each `TurnExecutor` in another process.

- A voice event reads the room's context for its hooks only when a hook is
  registered on one of its triggers, once for the whole event (RMK-797). An
  utterance announces ON_SPEECH_END, ON_TRANSCRIPTION and, with a turn
  detector, ON_TURN_COMPLETE or ON_TURN_INCOMPLETE: it read the room, its
  bindings and its participants before the STT whatever was registered, and
  its speech start read them again for ON_SPEECH_START. Partial
  transcriptions, VAD silences, barge-ins, DTMF, `say()` and recordings read
  them on every event too, in `VoiceChannel`, `RealtimeVoiceChannel` and
  `ConferenceChannel` alike (a conference also on each participant's speech
  start and end). Now the first trigger with a registered hook reads the
  context, the event's later triggers share it, and an event with no hook
  reads nothing. A voice turn with no voice hook reads the context twice
  instead of four times (the inbound pipeline's own reads, RFC §10.1 steps 3
  and 6, are unchanged): on `benchmarks/voice`, 12.9 µs per frame becomes
  11.4 µs on `InMemoryStore` and 23.8 µs becomes 20.8 µs on `PostgresStore`,
  where each read saved is a connection checkout and three SELECTs.
  `InMemoryStore.binding_exists` no longer deep-copies the binding it checks.
  An utterance whose ON_SPEECH_END observers cannot read the context (the
  room gone from the store, the store failing) skips them, logged, and goes
  on, since an ASYNC hook cannot block (RFC §9.3); an ON_TRANSCRIPTION hook
  that cannot read it still drops the utterance, failing closed. So an
  utterance whose room has gone from the store now reaches the inbound
  pipeline, which opens the room again as it does for any message naming one
  that does not exist, unless an ON_TRANSCRIPTION hook is registered; it
  used to fail on the voice side's read.

- The energy VAD, the energy barge-in check, the simple AGC, the realtime
  output-activity check and Speex's DEBUG statistics square a frame's samples
  with `math.sumprod` instead of a per-sample generator (RMK-796). The sums
  are the same integers, and the RMS of the VAD and the barge-in check is now
  the correctly rounded root, as the AGC's already was (it moves by one unit
  in the last place at most); the sum costs 2.3 µs instead of 5.1 µs on a
  160-sample frame (8 kHz, 20 ms), and a frame through the energy VAD costs
  RoomKit about 13 µs instead of 16 µs. `pcm16_energy` and `pcm16_rms` in
  `roomkit.voice.utils` are the one standard-library implementation, since a
  base install has no NumPy; the paths whose extras bring NumPy share
  `pcm16_energy_numpy`, an int64 dot that is faster on all but the smallest
  frames. `rms_db`, behind the audio-level hooks, moves to it from a float64
  mean: 1.3 µs instead of 2.7 µs on 160 samples, 2.2 µs instead of 4.1 µs on
  2400, the same values to 1e-9 dB; Sherpa's VAD and WebRTC's AEC already
  summed that way.

- A turn's stream costs the room's owner little per item across the turn
  backend (RMK-823, RFC §10.6.3, §10.6.4). Each `pull` grants a window of
  items, so the executor reads text and reasoning deltas ahead of the
  owner's reader, never past a call's start, a segment break or a round's
  end before the reader read it: a `Pull` says how many items its reader
  read (`read`), and one sent earlier grants nothing past such an item.
  Text deltas the channel yields without a wait between them cross as one
  `item`, their text joined and their number given (`deltas`). 2000 deltas
  yielded at once cost the owner's loop about 3 ms of CPU instead of 68 ms.
  A reader sees the same text cut differently:
  a voice channel's sentence budget reads a joined burst a sentence at a
  time, so it still stops before a call its next sentence would announce.
  Deltas read ahead that the reader had not read when the turn was
  cancelled or its stream closed are dropped, so the room keeps what was
  shown; a close that finds the executor reading ahead cuts that read at
  once, while a running call still finishes.

- Work a turn began reaches the room owner after the turn ended (RMK-827,
  RFC §10.6.3, §10.6.5). `current_turn_host()` keeps answering in it (a
  background thinker's `ON_THOUGHT`, a task a tool started), its host's
  `open` then false: `send_event`, `post_status`, `update_room_metadata` and
  `add_observation` cross as a `room_call` at the turn's chain depth, through
  a port the backend gives each executor it serves (`TurnBackend.attend`,
  `RoomOwner`; `TurnExecutor.reach_owner`); `delegate`, `wait_task` and the
  readers raise `RuntimeError` there. A realtime publication or framework
  event made after its turn crosses as a `room_publication`, published by the
  owner for the turn's room and kinds only, on the kit's executor as on a
  host's, where it was dropped. The owner accepts both only from the
  executor of the room's last turn of the channel, as it records it when the
  executor accepts the turn, a host verb only for that very turn
  (`PermissionError` otherwise) and at the turn's response depth it recorded;
  a closed owner refuses them. A thinker reports each thought under the turn
  that asked for it. `ScoringHook` writes its scores through the host, never
  the store itself, drops one with no owner to reach, and no longer needs a
  store to attach (`store=` is ignored). Example:
  `examples/thought_after_turn.py`.

- A discussion hands each committed message to its agents' memories through
  the turn backend, where each agent runs (RMK-827, RFC §10.6.3, §19.7.5 rule
  3): a `committed_event` channel control reaches the executor holding the
  agent's state for the room, else one that would take the room's turns (the
  room's hooks named), without moving the holder, and calls the new
  `Channel.on_room_event(room_id, event)` (an `AIChannel` hands it to its
  memory). It no longer calls the live agent
  object the kit holds, so an agent held by its declaration alone, or run on
  a host's executor, learns the conversation too. A discussion turn the speak
  policy leaves silent no longer hands its message to memory a second time.

- The tools orchestration sets up for an AI channel are kept by the room's
  owner, per channel and room, beside the channel's declaration, never on the
  live agent (RMK-826, RFC §10.6.2, §10.6.5): the handoff (`setup_handoff`,
  Swarm, Pipeline, `ConversationRouter`, `ConversationPipeline`), the
  Supervisor's `delegate_workers` and `delegate_to_<id>`, a delegation's
  `submit_result` / `submit_verdict`, `setup_background`, `setup_task_tools`
  and `setup_delegation`. The kit lists them in each turn it submits, as
  before. `AIChannel.extra_tools` returns the host's tools only. A tool given
  to a live agent under the name of an orchestration tool already set up for
  it is no longer refused when given: the executor refuses the agent's next
  turn instead, with `ToolNameCollisionError` naming the tool, as it refuses
  any turn whose owner tool its channel declares too (a host executor's agent
  differing from the kit's copy, or one the kit holds by declaration). The
  realtime installs stay on the realtime channel.

- Attaching an intelligence channel to a room, and detaching it, reach every
  executor that declares the channel through the turn backend (RMK-812, RFC
  §10.6.3: `RoomAttached`, `RoomDetached`). The executor calls the channel's
  `on_room_attached` / `on_room_detached` and logs what they raise: such an
  exception no longer cancels the attachment, nor reaches the caller of
  `detach_channel`. A channel of another category is called as before.

- **BREAKING — detaching an `ACPChannel` from a room closes the room's
  session and forgets the config values the host set on it** (RMK-812, RFC
  §10.6.3, §6.4): a later attachment opens a new session, caught up on the
  room, where it used to resume the old conversation. The detach never waits
  for the agent: the session is closed in the background once the room's
  running turn ended (a standalone turn's included, RMK-820), or by that
  turn itself when it prompted the room's session; a turn started before the
  detach that has not prompted yet ends without prompting, marked
  `interrupted`. Migration: a host that relied on a re-attachment resuming
  the agent's conversation keeps the agent attached; one that re-attaches
  sets its config values again with `kit.channel_call(channel_id, room_id,
  "set_config_option", config_id=..., value=...)`.

- Detaching an `AIChannel` from a room drops everything it keeps for the
  room (RMK-812, RFC §10.6.3): its plan, the images its provider refused, and
  its records of tools used and skills activated, which its next turn
  hydrates again from the store, beside the thought and the speak policy's
  state it already dropped. The executor drops the same when a turn
  elsewhere made the room's state stale.

- A turn the in-memory turn backend has no executor for fails at once with
  `TurnLinkError("no_executor")` (RMK-812, RFC §10.6.7), where it waited the
  accept timeout (10 s) for one to serve.

- The tools orchestration sets up are served by the room owner (RMK-811, RFC
  §10.6.5). A turn's request lists the ones set up for the channel in the
  room (`owner_tools`: a delegation's `delegate_task`, `work_in_background`,
  a handoff, a supervisor's `delegate_workers` and `delegate_to_<worker>`, a
  delegation's `submit_result`); the channel declares them from the request,
  not from its registry, and a call to one crosses as a `tool_call` the owner
  answers once with a `tool_result`. The handler runs on the owner, on a task
  of its own, in a copy of the context of the owner's task reading the turn
  and under the turn's id, under the call's context: the room and the channel
  of the request the owner submitted (a call naming others is refused), its
  `Room`, chain depth, actor, allowed names, requester and the call's id. Its
  `structured_content` comes back on the call. The call keeps the channel's
  bound on the executor; a call past it, or in a turn cut, is withdrawn
  (`call_cancel`) and the owner cancels the handler while the turn goes on.
  A handler that ends on a cancellation of something it awaited fails its
  call. A handler's error keeps its class's name (`ON_TOOL_CALL`'s
  `error_detail`, and what the model reads), one of a class outside RoomKit
  and Python included, and a structured copy JSON has no form for fails the
  call with a `TypeError`. On the owner a handler reads no response-metadata
  record: the turn's is the executor's. The kit's close waits for a handler
  still running to unwind, and a close a handler calls runs to its end.
  `TaskStatusTool` and `CancelTaskTool` given to an agent stay host tools
  (`setup_task_tools` has the owner serve them, RMK-825), and the owner keeps
  the tools it serves beside the channel's declaration (RMK-826).
  `OwnerTools` and `OwnerTool` are exported.

- **The hooks of a turn fire on the turn executor** (RMK-810, RMK-833, RFC
  §10.6.6): `BEFORE_AI_GENERATION`, `ON_AI_THINKING`, `ON_AI_RESPONSE`,
  `BEFORE_TOOL_USE`, `AFTER_TOOL_ROUND`, `ON_TOOL_CALL`,
  `ON_USER_INPUT_REQUIRED`, `ON_SPEAK_DECISION`, `ON_THOUGHT` and
  `ON_PLAN_UPDATED` fire where the turn runs. Registered on the kit
  (`kit.hook(...)`, `kit.add_room_hook(...)`, `kit.hook_engine.register(...)`)
  they are the kit's own executor's, as before: they fire for the agents the
  kit runs, realtime voice, conference and external tool calls included. An
  agent the kit holds by its declaration alone runs its turns on another
  executor, where such a hook would never fire, so the kit refuses with a
  `ValueError` naming the executor-side call a turn hook that agent could
  fire (its `channel_ids` can leave it out, and on a tool call or an input
  request its `channel_types`), and that
  agent's declaration while such a hook is registered; a room hook on a turn
  trigger is refused while the kit holds any declared agent. For agents run
  elsewhere, register on their executor: `executor.hook(...)` takes
  `kit.hook`'s options, and a room hook is defined by name,
  `executor.room_hook(name, ...)`, and enabled for a room with
  `kit.enable_room_hook(room_id, name)` (RMK-821); `kit.turn_executor` is the
  kit's own. An executor refuses the owner's triggers. `kit.remove_room_hook`,
  `kit.hook_engine.remove_global_hook` and
  `kit.hook_engine.FAIL_CLOSED_TRIGGERS` reach the kit's turn hooks too; a
  bare `HookEngine()` refuses the turn triggers. `ScoringHook.attach` and the
  console register on the kit's executor. `kit.hooks_for(trigger)` and
  `roomkit.TURN_TRIGGERS` serve code that registers on triggers of both
  sides.

- A strategy that takes an agent's turns runs on the room's owner, and each
  generation it asks of the agent is a turn of its own (RMK-814, RFC §10.6.1).
  The kit keeps the runners of a `Loop` and of a supervisor's delegation
  passes per room and agent, and an agent's solicited turn in such a room
  reaches the runner on the owner before it reaches the turn backend. The
  generations the runner asks of the agent itself (a supervisor's formulation
  and presentation passes; a loop producer's answer to an agent's or the
  system's message, or to one the loop's tasks cannot carry) cross the backend
  as turns marked `strategy_turn` and enter through the channel's `on_event`,
  which answers them past its speak policy and its thinker: a subclass that
  wraps `on_event` sees each of these generations, where it saw one call for
  the runner's whole turn. A loop's produce and review rounds stay
  delegations, turns of child rooms. The pass-1 instruction rides the turn's
  binding (`_turn_instruction` in its metadata) and the channel appends it
  after the prompt the turn resolves, where the supervisor resolved that
  prompt itself. `AIChannel.thinks_while_listening` says whether a channel
  carries a thinker, which a discussion refuses.

- A discussion's default rules ask for the handle wherever someone must act
  next (RMK-806): "Whenever another agent must act next, end your message
  with its handle, as in @dev: a name without @ reaches nobody, nor does "your
  turn" or "over to you" alone, in any language, and a message that names
  nobody wakes nobody." Told only that a name with `@` addresses another,
  agents on some models went on calling each other by their bare names, or
  handed over with "à toi" and no handle, and the discussion stopped.

- A model that does not see reads an image an author sent as
  `[Image not shown, this model does not see images: “lamp.png”]` (RMK-805,
  RFC §6.4), where it read `[Media: lamp.png]`: the label did not tell it that
  it could not see the image, and a small model answered as if it had. Like
  the other mentions, it names the image by its caption, else its filename,
  else its type, and nothing is resolved for it. A captionless image alone in
  its event now reads as that mention rather than as what
  `describe_empty_event` says, which still answers first for a captionless
  media that is no image. A document still reads as its label.

### Removed

- `roomkit.webrtc.utils.audio_to_bytes` and `audio_to_file`, never exported
  or called, and with them `pydub` from the `fastrtc` extra (RMK-824).

### Fixed

- The router skips a transport binding whose channel is not registered in the
  process without a warning (RMK-828). A transport reaches its client from the
  process the client connected to, and its binding outlives that connection:
  a host that keeps a client's binding between two connections, or runs
  several processes, held bindings with no live channel here, and every
  broadcast logged one warning per such binding with the whole registry in
  it. An absent intelligence channel the event solicits still warns, since
  an agent goes silent.

- A hook's channel filters hold on the triggers a turn fires (RMK-833, RFC
  §9.1): `channel_ids` and `channel_types` were ignored there, so
  `@kit.hook(HookTrigger.ON_TOOL_CALL, channel_ids={"support"})` fired for
  every agent's tool calls. They now read the turn's agent: its id, and its
  type when the trigger's payload carries it (a tool call, an input request).

- A cancelled delivery no longer reports its cleanup done while a turn it
  read still owes its end (RMK-823, RFC §10.6.8): once the owner's drain
  gave up at `cancel_timeout`, `cancel_and_wait` raises `TimeoutError`
  ("did not end on their executor") instead of returning; a cleanup nobody
  waits for leaves no unretrieved task error, and a turn the owner gave up
  itself, closing, owes nothing. A delivery that stops between its turns and
  their reader (cancelled once its plan ran, a root pass, or a delegated
  turn's commit or answer that fails) closes the turns' streams itself,
  rather than leaving them to the garbage collector while something still
  holds its result.

- A delegation requiring a structured result from a worker the kit holds by
  its declaration alone fell back to the worker's text: the result tool was
  set up on a live object the kit did not have (RMK-826). It is now set up for
  the worker in the owner's store, and its executor's turn is given it.

- `unregister_channel` drops the agent's auto-greet hook (RMK-822). An agent
  registered again under the id, or replaced by its declaration, kept the old
  hook beside its new one: a text room was greeted twice, and an agent
  registered again with `auto_greet=False` still greeted.

- `cancel_task` cancels only a task of the room of the call (RMK-825, RFC
  §23.4). It found a task by the status bus's `task` lines for the room and
  cancelled it by id, so a line any code holding the kit posted, naming
  another room's task, made a room's `cancel_task` cancel that task. The kit
  now records each running background task's parent room when it submits
  it, and a cancel for a room reaches only that room's. Its reach is
  narrower: a task a strategy runs unposted (`post_status=False`) or one
  submitted straight to `kit.task_runner` answers `unknown`, and is cancelled
  by `kit.cancel_task(task_id)`. A task whose end is being told reads ended.

- `roomkit[fastrtc]` imports on Python 3.13 (RMK-824). The vendored WebRTC
  transport used `audioop`, which left the stdlib in 3.13: directly in
  `roomkit.webrtc.websocket`, and through `pydub`. The extra installs no
  `audioop-lts`, so `import roomkit.webrtc` failed with `No module named
  'pyaudioop'`. The websocket's µ-law now goes through roomkit's own G.711
  codec, which produces the same bytes as `audioop`, and `pydub` is gone (see
  Removed). A CI job installs the extra alone on 3.13.

- The vendored WebRTC websocket drops a media frame over
  `MAX_INBOUND_AUDIO_FRAME_BYTES` before decoding it, as the Twilio and
  realtime websocket transports do (RMK-824).

- A cancelled delivery tells its turn's executor why (RMK-811, RFC §10.6.8):
  the cascade's reason (`superseded`, `caller_cancelled`, `kit_closed`...)
  rides its cancellation down to the turn and the turn's own work, a turn
  streamed to a transport included, where every turn read `cancelled`.

- An event a hook injects into a room where a strategy takes an agent's turns
  no longer runs the strategy (RMK-814): its delivery to a supervisor ran the
  whole delegation, its workers included, for an output nobody reads. It is
  delivered as an injected event is to any agent, its stream closed unread.

- A supervisor's workers' results reach its memory once (RMK-814): they were
  written to it directly, then again by the turn that presents them.

## [0.105.0] — 2026-10-16

### Added

- `await kit.room_strategy_is_current(room_id, Discussion)` tells a host
  whether the discussion this process installed is the one the room stores
  (RMK-779, RFC §19.7 and §19.7.5 rule 16). A process whose discussion another
  process replaced gives no turn, while `room_strategy()` still returns its own
  `Discussion`: once the process that replaced it stopped, the room waited and
  its host could not tell. False after such a replacement, when the process
  installed none, and once the discussion was uninstalled; the stored state is
  read when called, and an uninstall another process made is taken as soon as
  this process reads it, a discussion installed again since included
  (`room_strategy()` then answers `None`, where a replaced install still names
  the process's own). A host reinstalls only while its own state still wants
  the discussion. A strategy kind not stored with the room (`Pipeline`,
  `Swarm`, `Loop`, `Supervisor`) raises `TypeError`, so the question keeps its
  meaning if another kind comes to be stored.

### Changed

- **BREAKING — `install_strategy(room_id, Discussion(...))` over a room's
  discussion takes its place instead of refusing** (RMK-777, RFC §19.7). Over
  a discussion this kit installed (`install_strategy` or
  `create_room(orchestration=...)`) it raised `ValueError` ("holds a strategy
  already: uninstall_strategy() first"); it now replaces it and keeps the
  queue, an agent the new one leaves out cut mid-turn and detached when an
  install attached it (an agent the host bound itself is refused).
  `uninstall_strategy` in a process that installed nothing ends a discussion
  another process stored, in every process, and detaches the agents its
  installs attached, where it returned `False`. `Discussion.install(kit,
  room_id)` called directly now claims the room as every built-in strategy
  does: over a strategy the host recorded with `install_strategy` it raises
  `ValueError`, where both were set up side by side. Migration: a host that
  relied on the refusal to keep the first discussion checks
  `kit.room_strategy(room_id)` before installing; call `uninstall_strategy`
  only where the discussion should end for every worker; install over
  another strategy after `uninstall_strategy`.

### Fixed

- `uninstall_strategy` called while the host holds the room's lock returns
  when a discussion turn runs (RMK-778, RFC §19.7 and §19.7.5 rule 1). It
  waited for the cut turn's end to be recorded, which waited for the lock the
  host held: with `InMemoryLockManager` or `PostgresAdvisoryLockManager` it
  never returned and the room stayed locked for everyone (a lock manager that
  times out released it after its timeout, the end lost with a
  `TimeoutError`). Uninstalling now cuts the running turn and records nothing
  of its end, the queue being forgotten, without waiting for the cut turn to
  unwind (one that stored its text before a tool call writes its end on that
  message, under the lock), and no longer waits under the lock for the
  `ON_SPEAK_QUEUE` announcements, whose hooks may take it (that wait cost up
  to 10 s). A process that stops still records the end and keeps the queue.
- A discussion uninstalled by another process no longer comes back
  (RMK-778, RFC §19.7.5 rules 1 and 16). The turn running in the process
  giving the turns went on to its end and wrote the queue back into the
  room: a later discussion did not start fresh (its first pick read the old
  `last_speaker`). That turn is now cut once its process reads the queue
  again, and nothing of its end is written. Until then that process writes
  nothing back into the room either: a person's message there stored its
  ask, which a discussion installed later answered, and its lease, written
  into the emptied room, kept a fresh install from giving a turn for up to
  15 s; a task's result or an instruction reaching it meanwhile is posted or
  reported dropped. One case remains (RMK-785): an uninstall and an install
  again by another process, both before a process that installed the
  discussion reads the room (within its one-second poll, or while it is
  idle), go unseen there: that process stays installed and current, and the
  turn it was giving ends in the new queue.
- A discussion is installed, changed and uninstalled from any process
  serving its room (RMK-777, RFC §19.7 and §19.7.5 rules 1 and 16). After a
  restart, or on a second worker, `install_strategy` refused the stored
  discussion (`holds a discussion: no other strategy can join it`) and the
  room answered nothing; `uninstall_strategy` answered `False` and left it
  stored; changing the agents meant uninstall then install, which emptied
  the queue and left the other workers on the old agents, a message naming
  a removed agent answered by nobody on one worker and by another agent on
  the next. An install over a discussion now takes its place and keeps the
  queue, who listens and the turns given (see **Changed**). The agents
  installs attached are stored with the configuration, so
  `uninstall_strategy` in any process, one that only follows the discussion
  included, ends it everywhere and detaches them. Every process routes by
  the stored configuration as it changes; a process whose host installed
  another gives up the lease and only follows until its host installs the
  stored one, handing back the turns only it could give: the task results
  they were to post are posted, the instructions reported dropped. A
  process whose discussion another process uninstalled no longer keeps a
  strategy record without its discussion. A discussion stored by 0.104.0 or
  earlier names no attached agents: uninstalling it detaches none, from any
  process, the one that takes it back after a restart included, and an
  install that leaves out one of its agents is refused while that agent is
  bound (uninstall it, then install). During a rolling upgrade, a 0.104.0
  worker that installed the discussion keeps giving turns by its own
  configuration after a 0.105.0 process changed the agents, and drops the
  stored list when it stores its configuration: change the agents once
  every worker runs 0.105.0.
- An agent that only listens answers a person who names it (RMK-777, RFC
  §19.7.5 rule 12). Its turn was given, then cut at the first look the
  process giving it took at the queue, as if the host had just set it to
  listen: "@sre what do the metrics say?" to an `sre` that only listens got
  no answer whenever the model took longer than that look (50 ms to 1 s).
  Only setting the state while the turn runs cuts it now.

## [0.104.0] — 2026-10-15

### Added

- Fish Audio text-to-speech, Drama 3 by default (RMK-762,
  `pip install roomkit[fish-audio]`). `FishAudioTTSProvider` speaks
  `drama-3`, `s2.1-pro`, `s2.1-pro-free` and `s2-pro` over REST as streamed
  PCM and over Fish's streaming-input WebSocket (msgpack, one flush per
  sentence), voices a dialogue of up to four speakers in one render (a
  turn's `style` becomes a direction), and lists the account's voices then
  the public catalog. `FishAudioTTSConfig.expressive` performs the directions
  written in the text (`[calm]`, `[sigh]`, `<whisper>…</whisper>`); off, the
  text is spoken as written, brackets read as parentheses and markup read
  out. In both modes a control token in a text (`<|speaker:1|>`,
  `<|phoneme_start|>`) becomes a space, look-alike marks included, and so
  does a token with anything but letters and digits between its marks, which
  Fish drops before it reads (a zero-width space, an emoji, a format
  character such as U+0600): a forged speaker token in a quoted line switched
  the voice on every take. A text with no word to say is never sent, as a lone
  `[Calling a tool now]` made both model families invent up to 47 s of
  speech; on a stream it goes with the next sentence. An unknown model name
  is refused: the API would render it with s2.1-pro, and bill it so, without
  saying. Measured on the live service (2026-10-14): Drama 3's first audio
  arrives after 0.22 to 0.25 s over REST and over the socket (s2.1-pro 0.26
  to 0.31 s); Drama 3 costs 10 $ per million UTF-8 bytes against 15 $ for
  s2.1-pro, and speaks 40 to 60 % slower on the same text
  (`FishAudioTTSConfig.speed` compensates). Drama 3 is in preview: takes
  vary, a dialogue's change of voice included. Example:
  `examples/voice_fish_audio.py`.

- An image by reference, resolved by the application (RMK-763, RFC §6.4). A
  `MediaContent` URL may be a reference, `<scheme>://…` in a scheme the
  application chooses, naming a media it keeps in private storage;
  `RoomKit(media_resolver=...)` (`async (media, room_id) -> bytes | None`,
  exported as `MediaResolver`) gives every AI channel the bytes as it builds a
  turn, so the store and every broadcast keep the reference alone. The image
  then goes the way an inline one does: with its author's words, in later
  turns' history too, before the images tools returned. Any participant can
  write a reference, so a resolver answers only for the media of the room it
  is asked for. A transport channel is handed the reference as it is.
  Example: `examples/ai_image_reference.py` (offline, or `anthropic`: Claude
  Haiku 5.5 named the colour of a referenced swatch, then its shape on the
  next turn from history, 2026-10-14).

- A discussion's agents are addressed by handle (RMK-710, RFC §19.7.5 rule 4,
  §6.4). `Discussion(handles={channel_id: handle})`; an agent it leaves out
  is addressed by its channel id when that can be a name, else by its `name`
  kept to a name's characters (`Research Desk` gives `@ResearchDesk`). An
  application whose channel ids are `agent:<uuid>` had no addressing between
  agents: `@agent:3f2a…` reads as `@agent`, which names nobody; such an
  agent named `Jev` is now `@Jev`. The turn's notes, the label of an agent's
  turn in every transcript (AI and ACP context, memory summary, task brief),
  `DispatchTurn.speakers` and the classifier's team present agents by
  handle (`DispatchCandidate.handle`, new); the queue, `addressed_to`,
  `SpeakQueue` and every hook keep channel ids. `Discussion.handles()`
