  returns them; they are stored with the room, so a process that only
  follows the discussion reads them too, and a room stored without them
  keeps its channel ids. Background task texts (the worker's brief,
  the tool's answer, the relayed result, the tasks' block of the notes) name
  such an agent by its handle too, and so does `task_status` (`"agent":
  "Comms"`; `room_task_lines` keeps the channel id for a host, RMK-765).
  `DiscussionConsole` shows and reads agents by handle: the help, the cards,
  the status line, the notices and `/tasks` say `@Dev`, and `/listen @Dev`,
  `/talk`, `/task` read a name as the discussion does (RMK-764);
  `AgentCard.channel_id` (new) keys a host's own card whose handle is not its
  channel id. A `CLIChannel` with no `agent_label` shows every agent of a
  discussion room by its handle as the discussion writes it (`Dev:`, `@dev` in
  console mode, its banner included): such an agent showed as `Agent:8E41…`,
  and an agent whose channel id is its handle shows that id as written
  (`agent-researcher`) where a name was derived from it (`Researcher`)
  (RMK-766); a host's `agent_label` still receives the channel id. Example:
  `examples/discussion_group_chat.py`.

### Changed

- **BREAKING — a `Discussion` refuses, at construction, an agent no name can
  address** (RMK-710). A channel id serves as the agent's handle only when
  it is one: letters, digits, `_ . -`, at most 32, no final `.` nor leading,
  trailing or doubled `-`, not `all`. Otherwise the agent's `name` is kept to
  a name's characters, and with neither the construction raises
  `ValueError` where it used to build: `AIChannel("ai:support")` and
  `team/dev`, which no message could name (`@ai`, `@team`), and a
  36-character id or an agent whose id is `all`, each with no `name`. Two
  agents whose handles read alike ignoring case (channel ids `Dev` and `dev`)
  are refused too. Migration: pass `Discussion(handles={channel_id:
  "Support"})`, or build the agent as an `Agent(..., name="Support")`
  (`AIChannel` takes no `name`).
- **BREAKING — a turn sends the newest four images its authors sent, and only
  an image every vision provider takes** (RMK-763, RFC §6.4). Every image of
  the history window went before. History and input together now send four
  by default (`AIChannel(max_author_images=...)`, `None` for all), inline
  ones included, and only PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP up to 5 MB go as images, each
  under the type it was read as (`image/jpg` goes as `image/jpeg`, its data
  URI's header included): a HEIC photo, which Gemini took, and a JPEG over
  5 MB, which OpenAI took, now read as mentions. Anything else reads as a
  short mention, never a failed turn: `[Media: …]` for a document or for a
  model that does not see, `[Earlier image not shown: …]` past the bound,
  `[Image unavailable: …]` for a reference that does not resolve, `[Image
  refused by the model's provider: …]` after a provider error not retried on
  a request that carried it. `MediaContent` accepts a reference and still
  refuses `file:`, `ftp:`, `javascript:`, `vbscript:` and schemeless URLs,
  and a reference a path reader could follow (a one-letter scheme such as
  `C://…`, a `..` segment, a backslash); it now accepts a link or a `data:`
  URI whose scheme is in capitals and stores the scheme in lower case
  (`HTTP://…` as `http://…`), the spelling every reader tests. WhatsApp
  personal hands neonize a link or a `data:` URI's bytes and refuses a
  reference: neonize fetches only a lower-case `http://` or `https://` and
  opens any other string as a local file. Migration: `max_author_images=None`
  sends every image again; convert HEIC, and shrink an image over 5 MB,
  before it enters the room.
- `[Media: …]`, `[Voice message: …]` and `[Video: …]` (RFC §6.6) show the URL
  only when it is a link: a `data:` URI or a reference reads as the media
  type, where a text-only channel and a model without vision used to receive
  a whole base64 payload as text. A memory's summary and an ACP agent's
  catch-up read a media as the same label, and a composite as its parts.
- An `AIChannel` takes media whatever its model sees (its capabilities name
  `MEDIA`): the router no longer transcodes a media for a model without vision,
  the channel reads it itself, so a live captionless image goes to
  `describe_empty_event` first, as the same event in the history does.
- The images a turn sent, a tool's replayed or an author's, are dropped after a
  provider error only when the turn's first request failed, before anything of
  it streamed, on an error that is no authentication, payment (a 402),
  permission, missing model or rate limit (RFC §6.4). A key refused, an
  unpaid bill or a failure on a later round dropped them for the rest of the
  process.

### Fixed

- A Loop answers a message with a photo (RMK-767): a media, a text with a
  photo or an empty text got no answer at all (the loop rendered nothing).
  The producer now answers such a message alone and sees the media, as a
  one-pass supervisor does (RFC §19.7.4). The other readers of a message
  outside the AI channel read it as the AI channel does (RFC §6.6): a
  delegated worker's brief, the speak and discussion dispatch classifiers, a
  discussion turn's notes and a memory's summary read its text, `[Media: …]`
  and a voice message's transcript, where a media vanished and a composite
  lost its words; scoring no longer judges an answer against an older text
  message; a discussion's addressing and a memory's search read the author's
  words, a photo's caption and a voice message's transcript, never a file
  name.
- The AI channel reads a `RichContent` by its plain text, a voice message or
  a video in the history as the live event reads it (its transcript or
  label), and, for a model that sees, every part of a `CompositeContent`
  (RMK-767). Each read as nothing before; `describe_empty_event` is no longer
  asked about a `RichContent`, which now has text of its own. A memory's
  summary reads a voice message as its transcript or label, never its
  `data:` URI.
- A tool found through Tool Search stays declared once the model has called
  it (RFC §6.4). A second `find_tools` swapped the search window and took the
  called tool's schema off the wire with it: after `find_tools("dataset
  rows")`, a call to `tables_query_rows` and `find_tools("kanban boards")`,
  the next request declared `boards_list` and no longer `tables_query_rows`,
  so the model's corrected retry, or any later call, named a tool the request
  did not describe. A called tool now stays declared for the rest of the turn,
  including when its arguments were refused, without entering the memory of
  executed calls; on a provider that holds deferred tools unseen, that
  refusal carries the tool's reference. A realtime session keeps the schemas
  of the tools it called for its current catalogue, publishes them once the
  result is delivered, and drops them when the catalogue is replaced; a call
  from before a replacement cannot bring back a tool the replacement
  withdrew. Access refusals, skill gates and `BEFORE_TOOL_USE` still apply.
- The OpenRouter catalog prices `openai/gpt-5.6-sol` at OpenRouter's rate
  again: $4 per million input tokens, $20 output, $0.40 cached input and $5
  cache writes. Its $2/$10 promotion ended (read on OpenRouter's models
  endpoint, 2026-10-15), and a cost estimate on that slug read half the bill.
- A document sent as a `MediaContent` (a PDF, `application/octet-stream`) no
  longer reaches the model as an image the provider refuses: it reads as its
  label (RMK-763).
- An author's image a provider refused no longer fails every later turn while
  it stays in the history window: it reads as refused, as a tool's replayed
  image already did (RMK-738), and the turn's own author images are no longer
  spared while the tool images take the blame (RMK-763).
- A model that does not see no longer loses a media from the history: it read
  `""`, and a `CompositeContent` lost its text too, where the live event read
  `[Media: …]`. Both read the same label now; a captionless media alone in
  its event still goes to `describe_empty_event` first (RMK-763).
- The token estimate counts a document as its label, not as a 1000-token
  image (RMK-763).
- An image whose type is spelled `image/jpg`, in capitals or with parameters
  goes as an image again, sent as the type every vendor reads (`image/jpeg`,
  `image/png`), and an empty `data:` URI (a transport's failed
  download) reads as unavailable instead of failing a turn (RMK-763).
- A memory's summary no longer quotes a media's base64 payload or a tenant's
  storage reference, alone or in a composite: it read the content's repr
  (RMK-763). An edit whose new content is a media still does (RMK-772).
- A model file of the other family no longer ends the process (RMK-759): given
  `gtcrn_simple.onnx` under `model_type="dpdfnet"`, or a DPDFNet file under
  GTCRN, sherpa-onnx exited with code 255 on the first frame of a call ("Expect
  model type 'dpdfnet'. Given: 'gtcrn'"), out of reach of the provider's
  pass-through. `SherpaOnnxDenoiserProvider` now reads the file's ONNX
  `model_type` metadata when it is built (a protobuf walk that skips the graph,
  no onnx dependency) and raises `ValueError` naming the right type; an 8 kHz
  DPDFNet file is refused the same way on sherpa-onnx older than 1.13.5.
  `model_sample_rate` gives the rate the file declares.
- A new session no longer loads the denoiser's model again: `reset()` used to
  drop it, so each session start loaded it on the event loop (67 ms measured
  for dpdfnet2, about 20 MB). The model now waits for the next stream, its
  state reset (DPDFNet's `OnlineSpeechDenoiser.reset()`; GTCRN's runs keep
  none): the next session's first frame took 2.5 ms.
- A model that fails to load is reported once, then the audio passes through.
  The load was retried, and logged with a traceback, on every frame (about 50
  a second).
- The examples' `DENOISE=dpdfnet` takes the 48 kHz model on a 48 kHz pipeline,
  and is left out with a warning at a rate its model does not run; at 24 kHz it
  passed the audio through, logged as enabled.

## [0.103.0] — 2026-10-14

### Added

- `RealtimeAVBridge(on_video_detection=...)` receives what the filters of its
  `video_pipeline` detect: each `VideoDetectionEvent`, its `session` set to the
  call it was seen on. The callback may be async; a failure is logged and the
  video goes on. Without it the detections are drained and dropped (RMK-757).
  Example: `examples/realtime_av_bridge_detections.py`.
- DPDFNet denoises through `SherpaOnnxDenoiserProvider`:
  `SherpaOnnxDenoiserConfig(model_type="dpdfnet", model="dpdfnet2.onnx")`
  loads the DPDFNet models of sherpa-onnx's `speech-enhancement-models`
  release (`dpdfnet_baseline`, `dpdfnet2`, `dpdfnet4`, `dpdfnet8` at 16 kHz,
  `dpdfnet2_48khz_hr` at 48 kHz; sherpa-onnx 1.12.30 or later). It runs
  sherpa-onnx's streaming denoiser, which keeps the model's state from frame
  to frame: every frame comes back as long as it went in, and the audio trails
  the input by a constant 50 ms. On 5 dB SNR mixes of four speech clips, fed
  in 20 ms frames, `dpdfnet2` raised SI-SDR to 10.8 dB under the release's
  recorded noise and 11.5 dB under white noise, against 7.3 and 9.4 dB for
  GTCRN's sliding window, for 2.5 ms of one desktop core per frame (GTCRN:
  2.0 ms; `dpdfnet_baseline`: 1.5 ms). The offline denoiser, which GTCRN
  runs over a sliding window, cannot serve DPDFNet: it shifts the model's
  40 ms delay out of its result and pads the end with silence, so the newest
  frame always came back silent. A DPDFNet model denoises frames at its own
  rate only; frames at another rate pass through with a warning (sherpa-onnx
  ends the process when a stream's rate changes, so it never sees one). The
  silence gate stops the model after 100 ms of quiet input, so an utterance's
  tail still comes out. `model_type` defaults to `"gtcrn"`, so existing configs are
  unchanged; an unknown type, DPDFNet without `model`, or DPDFNet with
  `context_frames` is refused when the config is built. Example:
  `examples/dpdfnet_denoiser.py`; `DENOISE=dpdfnet` selects it in the other
  examples, which pass their audio through with a warning when they run at
  another rate than the model's.

### Changed

- **`play()` reports the playback it cuts, and `say()` and `play()` take over a
  response that only drains its echo instead of cancelling it** (RFC §12.2,
  RMK-747). `play()` used to start under whatever was playing; it now cuts a
  playback still being sent, as `say()` does, and `ON_TTS_CANCELLED` (reason
  `new_tts`) fires for it. A response sent whole whose echo is still draining
  (no AEC) was heard in full, yet `say()` fired `ON_TTS_CANCELLED` for it and
  flushed the audio still leaving the transport; it is now taken over as a
  response takes it over, with no event and no flush. A hook counting
  `ON_TTS_CANCELLED` sees one more for a `play()` over speech, and none for a
  `say()` after a finished response. A response still cuts a `play()`.

### Fixed

- `VoiceChannel.play()` no longer plays over the playback under way: a response
  or a `say()` playing when it was called kept streaming under the WAV,
  unreported. The WAV's audio is now measured as it goes out: a `play()` cut
  short reports the audio heard of it, and counts it toward the session's
  played total the echo guard reads, where it counted 0 ms (RMK-747).
- A session served by a backend added with `VoiceChannel.add_backend()` gets
  everything addressed to it through that backend (RFC §12.7.3). A response
  delivered to the room never reached it (its sessions were looked up on the
  primary backend only); a streamed response's audio and transcriptions,
  `send_dtmf()` and `disconnect_session()` went out on the primary; the cut of
  an interruption and the end of a playback read the primary's `INTERRUPTION`
  and `NATIVE_AEC`; `interrupt_all()` and the speech held during playback
  skipped it. The added backend's out-of-band DTMF now reaches `ON_DTMF` and its
  own barge-in detection is listened to; `kit.join(..., backend=)` starts a
  pull-model added backend listening (it told the primary), and records the
  video of a call on an added combined A/V backend (RMK-748).
- `SherpaOnnxTTSProvider.synthesize_stream` no longer leaves its reader waiting
  for good when the synthesis fails (an unknown speaker id, an ONNX Runtime
  error): the error is raised to the reader. A stream closed early (a barge-in)
  stops the synthesis at the sentence under way instead of waiting for the
  whole text. When `warmup()` was not called, the model is loaded in a worker
  thread, once, instead of on the event loop by the first synthesis (Kokoro
  reads ~126 MB) (RMK-749). `SherpaOnnxSTTProvider` loads its recognizer the
  same way (RMK-755).
- `RealtimeAudioVideoChannel` fires `ON_VIDEO_DETECTION` for what its video
  pipeline's filters detect, as `AudioVideoChannel` does; it kept each
  session's detections without ever draining them. A session's end resets its
  state in the pipeline once its vision analyses still under way are cancelled,
  frames arriving while it ends are dropped, and `close()` closes the pipeline
  and each vision provider once, the one given in `video_pipeline` included
  (RMK-750).
- `RealtimeAVBridge` drains its video filters' detections on every frame, where
  they piled up for the whole call (it has no hook to fire them on, so they are
  dropped), resets a call's video state when the call ends, and closes its
  video pipeline in `close()` (RMK-754).
- `RedisDeliveryBackend` hands a retry to a waiting worker as soon as its delay
  has passed. `dequeue()` queued the due retries once, then waited the whole
  timeout on new work, so a retry falling due meanwhile waited it out too: up
  to 2 s under the backend's own worker (`start()`), 5 s at the default
  `poll_timeout`, for a `retry_delay` of 0.2 or 1 s. The wait now ends when
  the next retry is due, by the Redis server's clock, and that call returns it
  (RMK-751).
- `find_latest_room` returns the same room in every store when several were
  created at the same instant: the one with the highest id, as
  `find_room_id_by_binding` and `find_room_id_by_participant` already did.
  `PostgresStore` compares room ids byte by byte (`COLLATE "C"`) in every room
  ordering, as the other stores do: on a database created in `en_US.utf8`, ids
  differing in case came back in another order (RMK-752).
- `InMemoryStore` no longer raises `TypeError` in `find_latest_room`,
  `find_room_id_by_binding`, `find_room_id_by_participant` and
  `find_room_ids_by_channel` when a room created with a naive `created_at` sits
  beside one with a time zone: rooms are ranked by timestamp, as `list_rooms`
  already did. `list_events` filters by `after_time` and `before_time`, and a
  thread summary dates its last reply, the same way (RMK-756).

### Security

- **A room's recording no longer receives the media of other rooms' sessions**
  (RMK-758). The audio and video recording taps sit on the channel's whole
  pipeline, or on a combined A/V backend's whole video facet, which every
  session of every room on that channel goes through, and they ignored the
  session a frame came from: with one `VoiceChannel` serving two recorded
  rooms, a call in one room was recorded in the other too, and within one room
  every session's audio, and the speech sent to it, went into every other
  session's track. Each tap now takes its own session's frames only.
  Recordings made with several sessions on one channel before this release may
  hold other sessions' media.

## [0.102.0] — 2026-10-14

### Added

- Kokoro speaks through `SherpaOnnxTTSProvider`, on the CPU or a CUDA GPU:
  `SherpaOnnxTTSConfig(model_type="kokoro", voices="voices.bin", lang="fr", ...)`
  loads the Kokoro-82M models sherpa-onnx packages (`kokoro-int8-multi-lang-v1_0`,
  126 MB: 54 voices in American and British English, Spanish, French, Hindi,
  Italian, Japanese, Brazilian Portuguese and Mandarin). `lang` names the
  espeak-ng language of text that is neither English nor Chinese: without it
  the multi-lang model reads French as English ("je suis votre" came back from
  Whisper as "Jisui, vente"); with `lang="fr"` the same sentence transcribed
  word for word. A voice is an index into `voices.bin` (`ff_siwis` is 30). On
  two threads of a desktop CPU the int8 model renders a sentence in about two
  thirds of its spoken length. `model_type` defaults to `"vits"`, so Piper
  configurations are unchanged; an unknown type, or Kokoro without `voices`,
  is refused when the config is built. Example: `examples/kokoro_tts_room.py`.

### Changed

- **BREAKING — `SIPVideoBackend`, `RTPVideoBackend` and `FastRTCVideoBackend`
  are no longer `VideoBackend`s** (RFC §12.8.3, RMK-723). They are
  `AudioVideoBackend`s: voice backends whose calls' video is served by their
  `video` facet, a `VideoBackend` whose sessions carry the call's id. Their
  own `on_session_ready` and `on_client_disconnected` report every call;
  `backend.video.on_session_ready` and `backend.video.on_client_disconnected`
  report its video. Migration: hand `backend.video` to whatever takes a
  `VideoBackend` (`VideoChannel("cam", backend=backend.video)`). A custom
  combined backend subclasses `AudioVideoBackend` (and `CallVideoBackend` for
  its video) to work with `AudioVideoChannel`. New in `roomkit.video`:
  `AudioVideoBackend`, `CallVideoBackend`.
- `ConferenceChannel.info` is a property, like every channel's `info`
  (RFC §6.1, RMK-724): code reading `channel.info` on any channel gets the
  map, where a conference handed it a bound method. Source-compatible:
  `channel.info()` still returns the map (see Deprecated); only a check such
  as `callable(channel.info)` sees the change.
- `InMemoryDeliveryBackend.get_dead_letter_items()` returns the most
  recently dead-lettered items first, as `RedisDeliveryBackend` does
  (RMK-725): with a `limit`, both now return the same items. The ABC states
  the order.
- Room pages come in the same order from every store, the oldest first: by
  `created_at`, then by `id` (RMK-726). `list_rooms()` and `find_rooms()`
  followed insertion order in the in-memory and SQLite stores, and
  PostgresStore left rooms created at the same instant in no set order, so
  a page boundary fell on different rooms.
- **BREAKING — a voice response no longer cuts the agent off**, a contract
  change 0.101.0 made without announcing it (RMK-704, RMK-735, RFC §12.2):
  every text the voice channel speaks as a response, an AI reply or a
  delivery, `Immediate` included, which used to cut the playback under way,
  waits until that playback has been sent whole, and `ON_TTS_CANCELLED` with
  reason `new_tts` no longer fires when a response reaches the agent's words.
  `say()` still cuts the playback under way, and the responses waiting play
  after it; a response cuts audio played with `play()`. Migration: to have a
  delivery cut the agent off, call `VoiceChannel.interrupt(session)` or
  `interrupt_all(room_id)` before it.
- **BREAKING — `DeliveryItem.max_retries` counts retries after the first
  attempt**, as `RetryPolicy.max_retries` does (RMK-722): 3 meant three
  attempts, it now means four. Migration: set it one lower to keep the
  number of attempts.
- SQLite files migrate to schema 6 the first time 0.102.0 opens them, and
  the migration is one-way (RMK-721): `read_markers` holds the event index
  (see Fixed), and 0.101.0 and earlier refuse a schema 6 file with
  `SQLiteSchemaError`. Copy the file first if you may need to go back.

### Deprecated

- The video methods of the A/V backends moved to their `video` facet
  (RMK-723): `get_video_session()` → `video.get_session()`,
  `list_video_sessions()` → `video.list_sessions()`, `video_capabilities` →
  `video.capabilities`, and `on_video_received()`, `add_video_tap()`,
  `send_video()`, `send_video_sync()`, `request_keyframe()`,
  `set_video_passthrough()` under the same names. The old ones still work
  and warn.
- Calling `ConferenceChannel.info()` (RMK-724): read the `info` property.
  The call still returns the map, and warns.

### Fixed

- `PostgresKnowledgeSource` indexes and searches in the language it is
  given (RMK-718). `language="french"` was stored and never read: both
  queries named `'english'`, so a French corpus was stemmed as English and
  a search for "cheval" missed a document about "chevaux". The language
  now reaches `to_tsvector` and `plainto_tsquery` as a parameter, and
  `init()` refuses one the database has no text search configuration for.
  A document keeps the language it was indexed with until it is indexed
  again: after changing it, index the corpus anew.
- A repeated `delegate_task` call answered from the cache gets what the
  task returned (RMK-719). Once a task completed, `DelegateHandler`'s cache
  kept the receipt of its start, `{"status": "delegated", ...}`, so the
  same call within the TTL was told the task was delegated, with no result
  coming any more. It now answers `"status": "completed"` with the task's
  `result`, as `task_status` gives it. With `serialize_per_room=True`, the
  handler also kept one lock per room it ever saw; the last delegation out of
  a room now drops it.
- `PostgresStore.update_room` refuses a room it does not hold and returns
  the stored `delivered_index`, as the in-memory and SQLite stores do
  (RMK-720). On a missing room it updated nothing and returned the room it was
  given; on a stale copy it returned that copy's delivery cursor, though the
  stored one, never written by this call, had moved on. It now raises
  `RoomNotFoundError`, and the room it returns carries the stored cursor.
- Read markers mean the same in every store: a channel's marker is the
  highest read event `index`, and it never moves back (RMK-721). Marking an
  empty room read on `PostgresStore` set a marker at 0, so the room's first
  event, index 0, arrived already read; an empty room now gets no marker.
  `PostgresStore.mark_read` took an event of another room; it now marks
  nothing. The in-memory and SQLite stores kept a position, not an index: the
  marker shifted when an earlier event was deleted and was wrong when events
  were written out of index order, and an older event marked read moved it
  back. SQLite files go to schema 6, `read_markers` holding the event index
  (one way: see Changed); a marker on an event that no longer exists is
  dropped, which reads as before (all unread). On `PostgresStore`, marking a
  missing room read now does nothing instead of raising a foreign-key
  violation, as the other stores do; a marker an earlier version set at 0 on
  an empty room cannot be told from a read of event 0, and stays.
- A delivery that failed is attempted again after a delay, not at once
  (RMK-722). `InMemoryDeliveryBackend` and `RedisDeliveryBackend` put a
  nacked item straight back on the queue, so every retry went out within
  milliseconds and the item was dead-lettered before a destination briefly
  unavailable (a voice session reconnecting) could come back. A retry now
  waits `min(retry_delay * 2 ** (n - 1), max_retry_delay)`, 1 s and 60 s by
  default as for a binding's `RetryPolicy` (RFC §13.2), both set on the
  backend (`retry_delay=0` retries at once). The Redis backend keeps a
  waiting retry in a sorted set (`{stream_prefix}:delayed`) on the server's
  clock; a worker queues it again once due, atomically. `get_queue_depth()`
  counts waiting retries, and `max_retries` counts retries (see Changed).
  Retries waiting when a process goes back to an earlier version stay in the
  delayed set, which that version does not read.
- A call on `SIPVideoBackend` reports itself to its channel, with or without
  video (RMK-723). The A/V backends were a `VoiceBackend` and a `VideoBackend`
  at once, two interfaces whose `on_session_ready` and
  `on_client_disconnected` share names and differ in meaning; the backends
  answered the video one. `ON_SESSION_STARTED` never fired for a call on
  `SIPVideoBackend`, an audio-only call's BYE left its channel bound (its
  pipeline and STT alive) and `RealtimeAVBridge` holding the call, and
  `ON_VIDEO_SESSION_STARTED` never fired on any of the three A/V backends.
  A call now reports `ON_SESSION_STARTED` once, and its video, when it has
  some, `ON_VIDEO_SESSION_STARTED` and `ON_VIDEO_SESSION_ENDED` once each.
  On `FastRTCVideoBackend`, a session's audio and video are reported live
  when its WebRTC connection is, not when the session is created; a session
  over WebSocket, which carries no video, reports no video.
- `SQLiteStore.find_rooms()` pages in SQL (RMK-726): it read and decoded
  every matching room, then cut the page in Python. With a
  `metadata_filter` it stops reading once the page is full.
- `update_room()` keeps the stored `event_count` and `latest_index`, in
  every store (RMK-727): a copy of the room read before events were
  committed took them back, and `event_count` never caught up. They are
  store-managed like `delivered_index`, and the room returned carries the
  stored values. `timers` stays the caller's: `set_room_timers()` sets
  `last_activity_at` through it.
- `PostgresStore.claim_voice_delivery()` refuses a room that does not exist
  with `ValueError`, as the other stores do (RMK-730), instead of letting
  asyncpg's foreign key violation through. The ABC states it.
- Gemini Live sees an image injected while audio flows: `inject_image` sends
  it as a video frame (`send_realtime_input(video=...)`) instead of `media`,
  the deprecated `mediaChunks` that `gemini-3.8-live` drops. Asked to
  describe a red circle and the number 42 shown that way, it answered "I
  can't see the picture you're referring to"; sent as a frame, it described
  both. `gemini-2.5-flash-native-audio` read the image either way. Checked
  live on 2026-10-14. A `prompt` sent with the image still reaches
  `gemini-3.8-live` before it has taken the frame in (it answered without
  the picture 3 times out of 3, the prompt sent before or right after the
  frame; one second after, it saw it): ask about an image in a later turn.
- `SherpaOnnxTTSProvider.synthesize_stream()` labels its chunks with the
  model's sample rate, as `synthesize()` already did, instead of
  `SherpaOnnxTTSConfig.sample_rate`. A config left at its 22,050 Hz default
  streamed a 24 kHz Kokoro or a 44.1 kHz Piper voice (`fr_FR-tom-medium`)
  slowed down and lowered.
- The voice response queue of 0.101.0 holds (RMK-735, RFC §12.2). Without
  an echo canceller, a session stayed "playing" for good after a streamed
  response, so every later final was discarded as its echo: the agent
  stopped hearing anyone. Responses waiting behind one playback all played
  at once when it was sent; they now take the session one at a time. A
  `say()` sent while a response waited played over it, and a response
  played over audio from `play()`; the `say()` now plays first, then the
  response, and a response cuts a `play()`. The drain of a playback cut
  short no longer ends the playback that followed it, nor hands on the
  speech the `DISABLED` strategy held while a response that took over
  plays. A playback that fails before its audio, and the playback of a
  session unbound or a channel closed, no longer hold the responses after
  them waiting for good. A `play()` under way reads as playing: waiting
  for playback waits for it, and cutting it is a cut.
- A later partial of an utterance taken for a response's echo no longer
  cuts the response that followed it (RMK-703, RMK-736, RFC §12.3.13).
  0.101.0 kept such words from deciding a barge-in on the energy path only;
  with responses now played one after the other, the STT's late partials of
  the first response's echo ("Je lance ça") landed on the second and cut
  it.
- With an STT that tells voices apart, a voice heard alone on a stream the
  provider closed no longer counts as a person's on the next one (RMK-706,
  RMK-737, RFC §12.3.13): each stream numbers its voices afresh, so a label
  carried over let the response's echo through as a turn. The rule 0.101.0
  brought in has a cost, now written in the RFC and accepted: a person not
  yet heard while nothing played who answers over a response with three or
  more of its words in their order ("the kitchen lamp" to "the kitchen lamp
  or the living room lamp?") cuts it and is not heard, so the agent stops
  and says nothing; what they say next while nothing plays is heard.
- An image a tool returned no longer blocks a room (RMK-708, RMK-738, RFC
  §6.4). 0.101.0 replayed any image, so one the provider refuses (a link that
  expired, an SVG, an oversized screenshot) came back on every later turn and
  failed it. Only an image every vision provider takes is replayed now:
  inline (a `data:` URI), PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP, up to 2 MB, from a live
  result, never one rebuilt from the store (the in-memory store handed seeded
  images back); and a turn that replayed them and fails on a provider error
  not retried replays none of the room's images after it. The images replayed
  are the agent's own tool calls' in the room. They count in what the turn
  measures before its history (RFC §20), a hook's `add_turn_note` joins the
  turn's one notes section instead of opening a second after them, their
  labels are cleaned of runtime-mark copies as the digest is, and the
  thinker's transcript no longer quotes their header as the participant's
  words.
- The tool digest no longer tells the agent that what it said came from a
  whole result (RMK-707, RMK-739): with the default eviction threshold, a
  large result reached the model as a placeholder on its own turn, and the
  sentence vouched for a guess. It now keeps what the agent said from a
  result it read whole.

## [0.101.0] — 2026-10-13

### Added

- An image a tool returned stays in view on the next turns (RMK-708). From one
  turn to the next the conversation keeps only a text digest of the tools used:
  a drawing or a screenshot was seen on its own turn and gone after, and "set
  the lights to that picture's colours" was answered blind. For a model that
  sees, the two latest images the room's tool results returned now ride each
  turn's input, after its notes, each after the call that returned it, framed
  as data a tool returned, never instructions; never in an assistant's
  message, where OpenAI refuses an image. Only images returned since the
  process started are kept: a result reloaded from stored history after a
  restart carries its JSON form, not its image. As the computer-use loop and
  other agent frameworks keep the last few, the bound holds each turn's cost
  (an image is a thousand tokens and more).
- Gemini 4 Argon, Google's new flagship reasoning model, is in the Gemini
  catalog: `GeminiConfig(model="gemini-4-argon")` (1,048,576-token window;
  text, image, video, audio and PDF input; thinking at `low`, `medium` and
  `high`; $2.00 / $10.00 per million tokens, $0.10 cached, through
  November 30, 2026, then $4.00 / $20.00 / $0.20). The model was already
  callable, but `GeminiAIProvider.available_models()` did not list it. It
  refuses `minimal` with a 400 and takes a thinking budget of 0, so turning
  reasoning off sends the budget (checked live).

### Fixed

- The local backend's echo canceller is told the delay the devices' clocks
  give, as browsers and LiveKit's console tell it (RMK-709). WebRTC's AEC3 was
  given PortAudio's nominal stream latencies once, added up: 296 ms on a
  MacBook, the input's alone 243 ms. Told a delay longer than the real one, it
  let the start of an answer through: the agent's "Salut" left at -39 dB of a
  -32 dB echo. `LocalAudioBackend` now gives an unset delay, on every captured
  frame, how long until the reference fed last is played plus how long ago the
  frame was captured, from PortAudio's callback timestamps
  (`outputBufferDacTime`, `inputBufferAdcTime`): 42 ms on that MacBook, and
  the start of the first answer at -64 dB. A delay set explicitly is left
  alone; a host API that reports no clock keeps the latencies' seed.
- An agent no longer takes back an answer because the tool-usage digest
  shows too little of the result it came from (RMK-707). Each turn replays the
  three latest results cut at 6,000 characters; a light's state stood past the
  cut in a 34,094-character list, and, told never to state a detail the
  excerpt lacks, the agent retracted the right answer it had given from the
  whole list. The digest now says to call the tool again before stating a
  detail it does not show, never to guess one, and not to take back what was
  already said from the whole result.
- With an STT that tells voices apart, the agent's own voice is no turn past
  the echo guard either (RMK-706). The echo canceller let "c'est bien la lampe
  Salon" through 20 s into a session; Meta heard "Eh bien, la lampe salon"
  from another speaker, and the agent answered it. A voice heard speaking
  while nothing played is a person's; a final from a voice never heard so,
  said over a response, whose words are that response's in their order, one
  misheard at most and three at least heard right, is discarded as its echo.
  The barge-in its first words decided still stands: the voice is known only
  with the final.
- A response no longer cuts the agent off: one that reaches a voice session
  while another plays there waits until that playback has been sent whole,
  then plays (RMK-704). A background task's result, relayed as the agent
  finished saying the task was under way, cancelled that sentence
  (`new_tts`), and the room, still ringing with it, barged in on the result
  before its first word. Responses waiting play in turn, each whole; the
  agent's words are cut by the person, never by its own next response. A
  playback sent whole whose echo is still draining (no AEC) is taken over
  without being reported cancelled, and its drain no longer ends the playback
  that followed it. `say()` still cuts the playback under way.
- Words taken for a response's echo decide no barge-in on another response
  (RMK-703). The STT never closed the echo's "Je": those words, still the
  utterance's, were judged against the next response, which does not say
  them, and the energy barge-in cut it at 0 ms. While the echo verdict holds
  they decide nothing; when it lapses with the utterance still open, they
  go with it.
- `work_in_background` asks the agent to say once that the work is under way
  (RMK-705). Told by the tool's answer to say it, an agent that had said it
  before the call said it again after.

## [0.100.0] — 2026-10-12

### Added

- Muse Wonder, Meta's preview model above Muse Spark, is in the Meta catalog:
  `MetaConfig(model="muse-wonder-1.0")` (1,048,576-token window, tools, image
  input, reasoning from `minimal` to `max`; $4.00 / $20.00 per million tokens,
  $0.20 cached; no contributor id). Meta's `/v1/models` already served it, but
  `MetaAIProvider.list_models()` kept only `muse-spark-*` ids and left it out;
  it now keeps `muse-wonder-*` ids too. Its `"none"` effort is refused by
  the service, as Muse Spark's, and sent as `"minimal"` (checked live).

### Fixed

- ElevenLabs streaming input never sends a chunk with no word to say on its
  own (RMK-698). The v4 models' dialogue socket refused one
  (`input_text_empty`), and the rest of the response went unspoken: an
  audio tag the model wrote before a tool call ("[Calling show_join_codes
  now]") went alone once the text before a call became its own segment
  (RMK-695), as did a reply ending on a tag. A chunk with no letter or digit
  (audio tags, spaces, punctuation, emoji, symbols, underscores) now waits
  for the next one, whose words it colours; one left at the end is not sent,
  so a reply ending on a lone "€" or "[laughs]" loses it. The speech socket
  (v2, v2.5) does the same, except that a tag's words are words to say
  there: those models read a bracket out.
- A response's own echo no longer cuts it at a session's start (RMK-697,
  RFC §12.3.13). A fresh echo canceller had heard nothing yet: the first
  response's opening words came back through the microphone (5 dB down), a
  streaming STT transcribed them ("Salut"), and the agent stopped; the
  echo's final, seconds later, came in as the person's turn. While a session
  has played less than `InterruptionConfig.echo_guard_ms` of response audio
  (6000 by default, 0 turns it off; audio played with `VoiceChannel.play()`
  counts), speech made only of words of the response being played,
  consecutive and in order, is its echo, whatever the strategy: it does not
  interrupt, is not queued, its partials are not published
  (`ON_PARTIAL_TRANSCRIPTION`), and its final is discarded, even once the
  response is over (up to 10 s after it). A partial's last word may be cut
  short after a whole word; a lone word, and a final, are matched whole, so
  "No" over "I'm not sure" cuts in. A word the response does not say makes
  it speech: when only the final says it, during the playback, the final is
  judged then and, if the strategy cuts, is the turn. A verdict ends with its
  utterance, its STT stream, or speech that starts once nothing plays. In
  continuous STT, while the guard is open, loud audio with no words yet waits
  for them up to `transcript_wait_ms` before it may cut on its duration.
  `InterruptionHandler.evaluate()` takes the response's text and the
  session's played audio for it (`response_text=`, `session_played_ms=`),
  and `InterruptionDecision.is_echo` says when it applied;
  `roomkit.voice.interruption.echoes()` is the test (`cut_short=False` for a
  final).
- A voice channel says the text before a tool call before the call runs
  (RMK-695, RFC §12.2 step 12s.a). The splitter held a reply's last sentence
  until a space followed its full stop, so "Let me check." waited for the
  tool and the model's next round, then ran on into its first word ("Let me
  check.It is 9."): silence for as long as a tool took. Each call's start now
  ends the text segment; the splitter lets out what it holds, however short.
  `split_sentences` and `filtered_stream` take a `SegmentBreakMarker` for
  it. At the marker, `filtered_stream` calls the filter's new
  `TTSStreamFilter.end_segment()`, never `flush()`, which stays the end of
  the stream's: it lets out the text the filter has decided to speak and
  keeps a span it removes open, so an `[internal]` block opened before the
  call and closed after it is never spoken. Its default lets out nothing, so
  a filter of your own keeps what it holds as before; override it if your
  filter holds text it has decided to speak. When the reply is said as it
  was read, the final assistant transcript and `AFTER_TTS` keep the segments
  apart, as `ON_AI_RESPONSE` does, a reply of exactly its sentence budget
  included; a reply a `BEFORE_TTS` hook changed, or a budget cut, is
  reported as said, one sentence after another.
- A sentence budget stops a reply of exactly its sentences that goes on with
  a tool call, before the call runs (RMK-695, RFC §12.2 step 12s.e): the
  voice channel did not recognise the call in the stream the framework hands
  it, so the call ran. With `max_sentences=1`, a reply that announces its
  call in one sentence ("Let me check.") now ends there and the tool never
  runs: give the budget room for the announcement if your agent makes one.
- `PhraseBackchannelDetector` lets more reactions through and still cuts on a
  hummed "no" (RMK-696). A player's « Ouh. » cut a story under semantic
  barge-in: `ENGLISH_BACKCHANNELS` and `FRENCH_BACKCHANNELS` now hold the
  continuers, agreement, assessments, surprise, disgust, laughter and thanks
  people say over a speaker (123 and 127 entries, from Switchboard counts,
  French CID and Québec CFPQ work, and voice-agent lists), Québec's « ouin »,
  « ayoye » or « mets-en » included. What asks the bot to stop or repeat,
  disagrees, doubts or opens a turn stays out ("wait", "huh?", "oh no",
  "really?", "that's true?", « hein », « voyons donc », « c'est bon »,
  « c'est vrai ? », « ben », « dis donc »), and so does an intensifier on
  its own: "very cool" and « trop bien » pass, « Trop ! » cuts. "mm-mm", the
  way Deepgram writes "no", read as two "mm" and let the bot talk on: a
  hummed no ("mm-mm", "uh-uh", "nuh-uh") in what the user said reads as
  "no", and a phrase list naming one never makes "no" an acknowledgement.

## [0.99.0] — 2026-10-12

### Added

- What an MCP server publishes on how to use its tools now reaches the model
  (RMK-692, RFC §21.2). `MCPToolProvider.instructions` keeps the
  `InitializeResult.instructions` a server sends when it connects (`None` when
  it sends none), and `MCPToolProvider.server_info` what it says of itself
  (`name`, `version`). `AIChannel(..., server_instructions={"gm":
  mcp.instructions})` and the same parameter on `RealtimeVoiceChannel` put
  them in every system prompt the channel composes, after its own prompt and
  before the skills: a prompt a binding or a `config_provider` sets for the
  room keeps them, Tool Search does not hide them, and no eviction or
  compaction reaches them. Each server's text is set apart as that server's
  data, in a `<server_instructions>` block under `## MCP server: <label>`, the
  label being the host's name for the server (ASCII letters, digits and `_ .
  -`, at most 64, else `ValueError`; anything but a mapping, or a server
  mapped to neither text nor `None`, raises `TypeError`), and is cut at 8192
  characters with a warning. A server mapped to `None` is left out, which is
  also how a host leaves one out. A realtime session whose provider takes no
  tools reads none of them. The `Agent` an `AgentReasoningBackend` drives
  reads its own in its model's prompt; a realtime pipeline refuses, at
  install, an agent that carries some, as it refuses an agent's skills, and
  names the voice channel's own `server_instructions=` instead (RFC §19.5).

### Changed

- PyYAML (`pyyaml>=6`) is a core dependency: every `SKILL.md` frontmatter,
  local or served, is read by YAML first (RMK-693). A local one YAML cannot
  read as a mapping is read line by line; a served one fails its check. The
  `mcp` extra no longer lists it.

### Removed

- `roomkit.skills.models.parse_skill_requires`, never exported: use
  `parse_tool_names`, which reads `requires` and, its glob reading aside,
  `allowed_tools`
  (RMK-693).

### Fixed

- A `SKILL.md` frontmatter that cannot be parsed names its skill: the
  `SkillParseError` reads `Parsing failed for <skill>: …`, so a strict
  `discover()`, which raises it as is, reports which skill failed (RMK-691,
  RFC §24.5). A validation error already named it.
- A served skill whose frontmatter holds a value its YAML tag cannot
  construct (`!!bool maybe`, `!!int ''`, `!!timestamp abc`) fails its
  check with `SkillVerificationError`, as any unreadable frontmatter does,
  where PyYAML's own `KeyError`, `IndexError` or `AttributeError` escaped
  it (RMK-691, RFC §24.7).
- `SkillRegistry.add_mcp_server()` refuses a label that ends in a line break
  (`"hf\n"`), as it refuses any label that is not an identifier: the check
  let a trailing newline through, which every served skill's name then
  carried into the prompt (RMK-692). A served skill's path is checked the
  same way, and so is a local skill's `name`: a skill named `combat\n` in a
  directory of that name loaded, and its name reached the prompt's skill
  list with the line break.

### Security

- **BREAKING — a local skill's `SKILL.md` frontmatter is read within the
  bounds a served skill's is** (RMK-691, RFC §24.5). It was read by
  `yaml.safe_load` with no bound, and every value turned into a string: 372
  bytes of YAML aliases of aliases became 254 MB of text, two levels more
  about 20 GB. It is now read by the reader that checks a served skill's
  frontmatter: a YAML alias (to an anchor defined before it; a `*` naming
  none, as in the glob `*_admin`, is not YAML and is read line by line),
  collections nested past 64 levels, more than 64 brackets or braces open at
  once (quoted ones counted too) and a frontmatter past 65536 characters raise
  `SkillParseError` before anything is built, where they used to load (a
  nesting past a few hundred levels was read line by line). `discover()` fails
  on such a skill, or skips and logs it with `strict=False`. A frontmatter
  YAML cannot read as a mapping is read line by line, within the size and
  bracket bounds.
  Migration: write the value in place of the alias.
- **BREAKING — a local skill keeps what it gates and requires, whatever its
  frontmatter looks like** (RMK-693, RFC §24.1, §24.2). PyYAML is now a core
  dependency, so a frontmatter that is YAML is always read as YAML. The base
  install, which had no PyYAML, read every local `SKILL.md` line by line, and
  that reading kept no list: `allowed_tools:` followed by `- item` lines was
  dropped, `allowed_tools: [search_*, fetch_*]` gated the patterns `[search_*`
  and `fetch_*]`, and valid YAML (a key nested under `metadata:`, a quoted
  key, a value continued over lines) could replace or hide what the top level
  gates. The tools a skill gates were offered to the model before any
  activation, those of the RFC's own example included. The line reader now
  reads only a frontmatter YAML cannot read as a mapping (a description with
  an unquoted colon); it keeps both list forms, items unquoted and a trailing
  `# comment` dropped, and of a text YAML also reads it gates at least what
  YAML does. An `allowed_tools` or `requires` neither reader can read whole as
  a text or a list of texts (a list spread over several lines, a block scalar,
  an anchor or a tag, a mapping or a nested list, a line under the key that is
  not a `- item`, a `\` escape in a double-quoted entry, a value or item
  opening on another YAML indicator: `{`, `%`, `@`, a backtick, or a bracket
  that does not close a one-line list, as in `[sw]earch_*`) raises
  `SkillParseError` naming the skill, where the skill loaded without the key
  or with it as one text. Read line by line, a top-level line opening on `!`,
  `&`, `? ` or `<<`, where YAML may read a key this reading cannot name,
  refuses the skill too, and a line indented under a key is left out: the keys
  of a `metadata:` block no longer reach `extra_metadata`. A `metadata:` block
  YAML reads is one `extra_metadata["metadata"]` entry, where the base
  install's line reading spread its keys there, so a `requires` nested under
  it requires nothing. Both keys read a value with one reader: a text `[a, b]`
  or quoted entries gate `a` and `b`, where `allowed_tools` gated `[a` and
  `'a'`, which match no tool, and a text in brackets also gates the glob it is
  (`[ab]` covers `a` and `b`), on every reader. A null list item no longer
  reads as the name `None` or `null`, local or served. A served skill's entry
  whose `allowed_tools` or `requires` is a mapping or a nested list is listed
  as malformed, as a local skill is refused, where its `requires` became one
  text naming a tool nothing serves.
  Migration: a skill that loaded with its gating lost now keeps its tools
  closed until it is activated; one refused needs its list written as `- item`
  lines or `[a, b]` on one line.

## [0.98.0] — 2026-10-12

### Added

- `SkillRegistry.add_mcp_server(server, label)` registers the skills an MCP
  server publishes under the MCP Skills extension, and an `AIChannel` serves
  them (RMK-682, RFC §24.7). Each is named `<label>:<path>` (`hf:hf-cli`),
  so it never shadows a host's skill or another server's, and nothing of it
  is fetched before it is activated. `activate_skill` then reads its
  `SKILL.md` from its own server and checks it against the entry (length,
  SHA-256, frontmatter field by field); the body reaches the model as that
  server's data, in a `<skill>` block naming its origin, after the host's
  own skills and never among their binding rules. `read_skill_reference`
  reads only a file the entry lists, from the same server, verified; a file
  that fails retires the skill, which the model activates again. A skill the
  listing did not hold is asked of its server by name (`skills/get`). An
  entry the extension does not allow, one past its limits and a dynamic one
  (unless `allow_dynamic=True`) are listed as unavailable with their reason,
  an entry read again after a failed check included. A registry and its
  copies share the servers' entries: a skill one of them retires is retired
  in each. A served skill's `allowed_tools` grants nothing, its scripts
  never run, and an activation is not replayed from the stored history. New:
  `SkillRegistry.load_skill()`, `read_file()`, `is_served()`, `origin()`,
  `has_served`, `execution_tool_patterns`; `MCPSkill`, `MCPSkillServer` (what
  `add_mcp_server` takes), `ServedOrigin`, `SkillChangedError`,
  `SkillVerificationError`.
- While a skill an MCP server serves is active in a conversation, a tool
  that runs code is served only with the host's approval of that skill
  (RMK-684, RFC §24.7): a sandbox command, `run_skill_script`, and the
  host's own tools named in `add_mcp_server(..., execution_tools=[...])`.
  The host answers through `add_mcp_server(..., approve_execution=...)`, an
  `ApproveExecution` callback that receives a
  `SkillExecutionRequest` (the skill, its server's label, its URI, the
  conversation, the tool, and the fingerprint of the skill's files); an
  approval holds for that conversation and fingerprint only, so a skill
  whose files changed is asked again, and a dynamic skill every time.
  Without a callback, such a call is refused. On `AIChannel` and
  `RealtimeVoiceChannel` alike.
- A `RealtimeVoiceChannel` serves the skills an MCP server publishes as an
  `AIChannel` does (RMK-683, RFC §24.7): an activation loads and verifies
  the skill, its body enters the session's instructions as its server's
  data, a fixed provider takes it in the activation's result set apart the
  same way, and a file that fails retires it in the session. In
  `inline_full` mode, which loads every skill's instructions when the
  session starts, a served skill is listed as unavailable, with that reason.
- `MCPToolProvider.server_extensions` and `MCPToolProvider.request()`
  (RMK-681, RFC §21.2): the extensions a server declared when it connected,
  and a request the MCP SDK does not model, returned as the server sent it,
  its null fields left out.
  They are what a registry needs to serve the skills an MCP server publishes
  under the MCP Skills extension (`io.modelcontextprotocol/skills`,
  SEP-2640), and rely on nothing a session alone holds. `roomkit.skills.mcp`
  reads one entry of such a server on its own (`parse_entry`, `SkillEntry`,
  `SkillResource`, the extension's 512-file and 16 MiB limits) and checks
  what the server serves against it: `verify_skill_resource` (length, then
  SHA-256) and `verify_frontmatter` (field by field). A frontmatter past
  64 KiB, in the entry's JSON as in `SKILL.md`, is refused, and so is a YAML
  one holding an alias, collections nested past 64 levels (flow or block) or
  a value JSON cannot hold: aliases of aliases expand exponentially, nesting
  deep enough overflows the C loader's stack and ends the process, and the
  server controls the digest too. Checked against
  `huggingface.co/mcp`: its 25 skills list over a `2025-11-25` session and
  verify. The `mcp` extra now brings PyYAML, which the frontmatter check
  needs.

### Changed

- **BREAKING — a delegation's child room belongs to its parent room's
  organization** (RMK-686, RFC §17.2, §23.3 step 1). `kit.delegate()` created
  the child room without an `organization_id`, so what acts in it read none:
  a tool reading `current_tool_room().organization_id`, a hook or a provider
  reading `RoomContext.room.organization_id` got `None` for a task started
  from a tenant's room, and code that filters by tenant only when it has one
  ran the task's work, and the parent's messages a `conversation=` hand-over
  quotes in its description, across every tenant; a verification a tool
  requested from the child room was opened outside the tenant. The child
  room now takes the parent's `organization_id`, a nested delegation's
  included; a room without one still has a child without one. A read or a
  verb scoped to the parent's organization finds the child room, one scoped
  to another does not, and `store.find_rooms(organization_id=...)` now lists
  a tenant's task rooms beside its own, counted toward its `limit`.
  Migration: where a list must show a tenant's conversations only, leave out
  the rooms whose `metadata["parent_room_id"]` is set; a `_child_metadata`
  envelope stamped only so the child room would carry the tenant can go:
  read `room.organization_id` instead.
- **BREAKING — `SkillRegistry.add()` refuses a skill name holding `:`**
  (RMK-682, RFC §24.7), with `SkillValidationError`: `<label>:<path>` names a
  skill an MCP server serves, which a host's skill must never shadow. A skill
  built in memory under such a name was registered before. Migration: rename
  it; a skill discovered from a directory never held one.
- An active skill the registry can no longer return leaves the conversation's
  active set as its body leaves the prompt (RMK-682, RFC §24.4). Behaviour
  change: a host's skill marked unavailable while active stayed active with
  no body in the prompt, and once registered again its body came back
  without an activation; it now leaves the active set, and its next
  activation delivers its body.

### Fixed

- A pipeline AEC fed by `LocalAudioBackend` in realtime mode keeps running
  between responses (RMK-678, RFC §12.3.4). It was bypassed at the end of
  each response's playback while the backend went on reporting the silence
  it played; WebRTC AEC3 dropped that reference while capture ran on, and
  came back at the next response with its timelines out of step. The echo it
  left reached the provider, whose server VAD took it for the user and cut
  its own reply (a recorded session replayed through AEC3: the next
  response's echo 0 to 5 dB below the microphone, against 34 to 44 dB kept
  running). The backend now marks each played block `reference_continues`,
  and the pipeline keeps the canceller active through a response's end when
  it does. A backend that does not mark its blocks so is bypassed there as
  before: SIP's, whose played blocks stop between responses unless
  `outbound_silence_fill=True`.
- `AnthropicAIProvider` sends the turn's `reasoning_effort` (RMK-676, RFC
  §6.7). It went nowhere: an `AIChannel(reasoning_effort="low")` on Claude
  ran at the model's default effort. It now rides `output_config.effort` as
  the nearest level the model takes, as the catalogue declares them from
  what the wire took on 2026-10-12: Anthropic's `xhigh` and `max` where the
  model takes them, `xhigh` as `high` on Claude Opus 4.6, Sonnet 4.6 and
  Opus 4.5, `max` as `high` on Opus 4.5 (tags `effort_no_xhigh`,
  `effort_up_to_high`), and the turn's `minimal`, which no Claude model
  takes, as `low`; a model the catalogue does not carry is sent the turn's
  effort on Anthropic's levels, and an effort outside them goes nowhere. It
  rides a turn with tools as one without, beside the answer's schema when
  there is one. `none` is not a level: it states reasoning off (next entry).
  Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Claude Haiku 4.5 answer 400 to the parameter: the
  catalogue tags them `effort_refused` and they are sent none, as before.
- `AnthropicAIProvider` turns reasoning off where the turn states it
  (RMK-677, RFC §6.7). A turn with `thinking_budget=0`,
  `enable_thinking=False` or `reasoning_effort="none"` left `thinking` out,
  which is off on Claude Opus 4.8 and earlier but not on the models that
  reason by default: Claude Opus 5, Sonnet 5, Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5
  and Fable reasoned anyway. The catalogue now declares how each one is
  turned off, measured on the wire: `{"type": "disabled"}` on Opus 5,
  Sonnet 5 and Haiku 5.5; `{"type": "between_tools"}` on Sonnet 5.5, which
  refuses `disabled`; and the lowest effort, `low`, on Opus 5.5, Fable 5.1
  and Fable 5, which refuse both and cannot stop reasoning (and on Mythos 5.1
  and Mythos 5, as Anthropic documents them, not measured). With reasoning
  off, Opus 5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 answer 400 to an effort above
  `high`, so `xhigh` and `max` go as `high` there. A model the catalogue
  does not carry is sent no `thinking` block for off, as before.

## [0.97.0] — 2026-10-11

This release lets several agents and people hold one conversation in a room:
a `Discussion` gives the turns one at a time, a dispatch policy picks who
answers a message that names no one, long work runs as a task off the floor,
and an external agent over ACP takes its turns like any other. Identity
verification tells the agents when the person writing has proven who they
are, and holds what they write until then. 3 of the changes below are
breaking; each states its migration.

### Added

- `Discussion` orchestration strategy (RMK-665, RFC §19.7.5): several
  agents and people hold one conversation in a room, any agent addressing
  any other by `@channel_id`, one agent speaking at a time. The strategy
  queues the agents each message asks for (a person's names first, else the
  agents that asked that person, else `everyone`; `addressed_only=True` asks
  only the named) and gives each turn as a rerun of the event it answers,
  reading the room as it is when the turn starts, bounded by its own
  `max_depth`. An agent with nothing to add answers its `silent_token`
  (`"(silent)"`), stored `BLOCKED` as `discussion_silent` and never
  streamed. `max_turns` and `done` end it. Each agent's memory provider is
  handed every message the agent may see as it commits, as in a room with
  no discussion, so a memory that learns as messages arrive (a retrieval
  index, a summary) learns the whole conversation. `kit.speak_queue()`,
  `kit.listen_only()`, `kit.talk_again()` and the new `ON_SPEAK_QUEUE` hook
  (`SpeakQueue`, `SpeakQueueChange`, `SpeakQueueEvent`) let a console follow
  who speaks, who is next and whether the room waits for a person. The room
  is the discussion's: while it holds it, `attach_channel` refuses another
  intelligence channel or a voice or realtime channel, a
  `ConversationRouter` hook is refused there (and as a global hook while
  any room holds a discussion), and `Loop`, `Pipeline`, `Supervisor` and
  `Swarm` refuse to install there. Text only. Example:
  `examples/discussion_group_chat.py`.
- A discussion is served by several processes sharing one store and one
  lock manager (`PostgresStore` with `PostgresAdvisoryLockManager`)
  (RMK-665, RFC §19.7.5 rule 16).
  - Its configuration and speak queue are stored with the room. Every
    process serving the room follows them, even one whose host did not
    install the discussion: it asks no agent at broadcast, reads names and
    queues turns, under the room lock.
  - One process that installed the discussion gives the turns under a 15 s
    lease it renews; another that installed it takes over once the lease
    expires.
  - An instruction's turn moves the lease to the process holding its text.
  - Example: `examples/discussion_two_workers.py`.
- A discussion's dispatch policy (RMK-666, RFC §19.7.5 rule 18):
  `Discussion(dispatch=...)`: a person's message that names no agent goes to
  the agents the policy picks, in its order, or to none (a thanks, small
  talk), in place of the agents that asked that person, else every agent of
  `everyone`. The policy is told which agents wait for the person's answer,
  so it tells an answer from a new request or a thanks. Not with
  `addressed_only`. `ClassifierDispatchPolicy` asks a classifier one yes/no
  question per agent in one call (Jev: about 150 ms); `MockDispatchPolicy`
  scripts decisions. The lease holder decides off the room lock, before its
  next turn, keeping the message's place in the queue; a failure or
  `dispatch_timeout` (5 s) leaves the message to the rule without a policy.
  The new `ON_DISPATCH_DECISION` hook reports each decision
  (`DispatchDecisionEvent`). On eight unaddressed messages to four agents,
  live on Jev: 8 turns and 2 silent ones, against 32 and 26 without a
  policy, for the same answers. Example: `examples/discussion_dispatch.py`.
- `OpenAIClassifier` (RMK-667, RFC §6.8): a classifier on OpenAI's Decisions
  API (`POST /v1/decisions`, public beta, `gpt-6-luna`), which answers
  yes/no, choice and score questions with probabilities, ~150–450 ms for the
  whole call. It serves `ClassifierSpeakPolicy` and
  `ClassifierDispatchPolicy` as `JevClassifier` does. A structured state
  goes as its JSON; a question the API declines fails the call with
  `ClassifierError`. No new dependency: the `openai` extra, through the SDK
  client's generic `post`. `CLASSIFIER=openai` in
  `examples/classifier_judgments.py`, `examples/speaking_judgments.py` and
  `examples/discussion_dispatch.py`.
- An external agent over ACP takes a discussion's turns like an AI channel
  (RMK-670, RFC §6.4, §19.7.5): `Discussion(agents=[...])` accepts an
  `ACPChannel`. `ACPChannel` takes `name`, `role` and `description`, its
  identity as an Agent's, and `instructions`, the standing direction its
  system prompt would give, sent once per session. A discussion's turn closes
  its prompt with the turn's notes under the runtime's header (a copy of the
  header anywhere else in an `ACPChannel` prompt is replaced), and
  `listen_only` while it speaks cancels its prompt, or its session's
  opening. Live, Claude Code answered as @dev, passed its turn when it had
  nothing to add, and was cut within 6 s of a hold.
- Long work runs as a task, off a discussion's floor (RMK-668, RFC §23.3,
  §23.4, §19.7.5 rule 19). `kit.setup_background(agent, *, worker=None,
  hand_back="relay")` gives an AI channel the `work_in_background` tool: it
  starts the work as a task on its worker (itself, another agent, an
  external agent over ACP), handed the room's last 12 messages, says it is
  on it and ends its turn. The tool starts tasks for its own agent only: a
  model never runs another agent's worker nor has a result come back in its
  name. `kit.start_task(room_id, agent_id, task, *, hand_back=None)` starts
  the same task from the host, for any agent of the room. In a discussion a
  question asked while a task runs is answered in its turn, and the result
  comes back at the front of the queue. `delegate()` gains `brief` (what the
  worker is told; `task` stays the label the result is named by),
  `conversation` (the room's last messages the notified channel may read,
  quoted as data) and `hand_back`: `"relay"`, the default, or `"post"`, the
  result published as the notified agent's message with no turn of its
  model, waiting at the front of a discussion's queue and asking no one
  (`ValueError` with `wait=True`, or when the notified channel is not an
  intelligence channel of the room). Live, a quick question asked during a
  long job was answered in 3 to 6 s instead of 31 to 49 s. A custom
  `TaskRunner` should give the worker `task.description` (the brief, else
  the task, with the conversation); `task.task` is the label. One that reads
  `task.task` runs a plain `delegate()` as before, but drops a brief and the
  conversation, which `work_in_background` and `start_task` rely on.
  Examples: `examples/discussion_background.py` (offline),
  `examples/discussion_acp.py`.
- `DiscussionConsole` (RMK-665, RMK-671; `roomkit.console`, `console`
  extra): a full-screen terminal on a room a discussion holds. The room on
  the left (messages, tool calls, who asks you, and, through a WebSocket
  channel, the answer an agent is writing as it streams), the agents on the
  right with their identity, model, live state (speaking, next, listening,
  asking) and running tasks, the speak queue below, your input at the
  bottom. `/listen` and `/talk`, the host's own slash commands, and, when
  an agent of the room has background work set up (or `tasks=True`),
  `/task @agent ...`, `/tasks` and `/cancel <task>`. A posted result names
  the worker that wrote it; an `ACPChannel`'s card reads "external agent
  (ACP)". The kit's logs go to a file while the screen is up. It follows
  the room through hooks it removes when it closes. Example:
  `examples/discussion_console.py`.
- `kit.install_strategy(room_id, strategy)` and
  `kit.uninstall_strategy(room_id)` (RMK-665, RFC §19.7):
  - A room holds one strategy at a time, and can change it while it lives.
    `create_room(orchestration=...)` installs through the same path.
  - An install on a live room registers and attaches the strategy's agents,
    as `create_room(orchestration=...)` does, and keeps the timeline. A
    strategy's own `install(kit, room_id)`, called directly, attaches none:
    a `Swarm` installed that way hands off to agents that are not in the
    room.
  - An uninstall runs the strategy's new `Orchestration.uninstall()` step,
    then takes back what its install added: room hooks, tools and turn
    runners on the agents, agents it attached, room metadata it wrote. This
    holds for a host's own strategy too.
  - A room a strategy was installed in through `install_strategy` or
    `create_room` refuses a second one until `uninstall_strategy`.
    `kit.room_strategy()` names the installed one, and
    `kit.claim_room_strategy(room_id, strategy)` is the check a strategy
    installed by calling its `install` directly makes (the built-in ones
    do); it records nothing.
  - A room created again with an id whose room was deleted takes back the
    strategy recorded for the old room first: its hooks no longer serve the
    new room beside the new strategy's.
  - Example: `examples/strategy_on_the_fly.py`.
- An `ACPChannel` sets each session up for its room (RMK-673, RFC §6.4, ACP
  agent channel, *Session setup*). `mcp_servers` also takes a function of
  the room id (`MCPServersForRoom`), sync or async, called each time a
  session opens for that room: a stdio server can be told its room in its
  `env`. `ACPChannel(session_config={"mode": "default"})` is set on every
  session the channel opens before it is prompted: the room's first, one
  rebuilt after a recovery or opened after the agent restarted, a standalone
  turn's and a task's child room's. A value the agent refuses fails the
  opening: the session is released and never prompted, and the turn fails
  with a `RuntimeError` naming the option. Example:
  `examples/acp_room_mcp.py`.
- Identity verification (RMK-660, RFC §11.7; guide: Identity Verification):
  identification says whose an address is, verification that the person
  writing has proven it. RoomKit keeps the state and its lifecycle; the
  integrator keeps the method (a page and a PIN, a login). Example:
  `examples/identity_verification.py`.
  - Requests: `kit.request_verification(identity_id, room_id=, channel_id=,
    method="link"|"code")` returns the request and its secret, once (256
    bits for a link, 6 digits for a code). The secret is stored only as its
    scrypt hash: a 6-digit code read from a leaked store takes hours to
    find, against its five minutes of life. A request takes its room's
    organization (a caller acting for another gets `RoomNotFoundError`), and
    a new request cancels the open one.
  - Completion: once its own check passed, the integrator calls
    `kit.complete_verification(request_id, secret)`. It refuses a request
    unknown in the caller's organization, no longer open, expired, or given
    a wrong secret (`VerificationRefusedError.reason`).
    `kit.record_failed_attempt(request_id)` counts the integrator's own
    failed check (a wrong PIN on its page) against the same bound, so a PIN
    cannot be guessed through the page. The last allowed failure fails the
    request. A request that fails while the identity is verified ends that
    verification too: whoever could not prove it is not let on as the
    person.
  - State and end: `kit.verification_of()` reads `UNVERIFIED`, `PENDING`,
    `VERIFIED`, `EXPIRED` or `REVOKED`, per identity and organization. A
    message is labelled by its room's organization's verification, so one
    proven to an organization never verifies the person in another's
    conversation. `kit.revoke_verification()` ends a verification and
    cancels the open request, so a link sent before it never verifies. A
    verification ends **when it expires**, by a timer armed at completion,
    and so does a request left unanswered. `kit.check_verifications()` ends
    what expired while nothing ran and re-arms the rest; `async with
    RoomKit(...)` calls it as the kit starts (a store that cannot answer is
    logged and the kit starts all the same), and `kit.close()` stops the
    timers. Lifetimes and attempts come from
    `RoomKit(verification_policy=VerificationPolicy(...))`. Framework
    events: `verification_requested`, `verification_completed`,
    `verification_ended`. `ON_VERIFICATION_COMPLETED` and
    `ON_VERIFICATION_ENDED` (ASYNC) fire in the request's room; an end names
    what ended (`ended`: `"verification"` when the one in force ended,
    `"request"` when only a request did, such as a link left unanswered).
  - Inbound (RFC §10.1 step 5b), on only when a `verification_policy` is
    passed; without one the pipeline is unchanged. An identified sender's
    message carries `source.verification`. While the identity is not
    verified, the message fires `ON_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED` (SYNC), and its
    hooks hold it (the default: visibility `"transport"`, so the room's
    people see it and no agent does, in delivery or in context), pass it
    (`HookResult.allow_unverified()`; a plain `allow()` does not, so a hook
    that only watches never lets one through) or block it. Holding only
    narrows what a message reached: the transports of its scope, never a
    channel it did not reach. An edit or a deletion from an unverified
    sender is refused (`verification_required`) unless a hook passes it.
    `kit.sender_verification(event, context)` tells a hook whose
    verification it is and whether a request is open, on the first message
    too. `VerificationPolicy(hold_unverified=False)` only labels. A reply
    that is the code of the sender's open code request in the room is
    consumed: it completes or counts an attempt, and is never stored nor
    broadcast.
  - Release (RFC §11.7.6): when a request completes, what its sender wrote
    while it was open gets back its visibility (`ON_EVENT_UPDATED`). The
    room's agents answer the last such message as its author's own turn, the
    earlier ones as its context, even if the host wrote after it. Nothing is
    copied, nothing becomes an instruction. Only what the pipeline held is
    released: from `window_start`, at most `release_max_messages` within
    `release_max_age`, never twice; `release_on_verify=False` keeps them
    held. The pipeline strips a held marker a sender's metadata carries, so
    no one slips a message into another's release.
  - Stores: memory, SQLite (schema v5, migrated on open for every SQLite
    file; 0.96.1 cannot open a v5 file) and Postgres keep it.
    `ConversationStore` gains the operations without making them abstract,
    so a store of your own keeps working and refuses them by name.
- `MCPToolProvider(..., discover=False)`, also on `from_url` and
  `from_command`, connects without listing the server's tools (RMK-662, RFC
  §21.2): a host that only reads a resource (an MCP App's HTML) skips the
  catalogue. `get_tools()` and `tool_meta()` are then empty, no call is
  checked against an output schema, and `as_tool_handler()` serves no tool
  (every call raises `UnservedToolCallError`);
  `as_tool_handler(gate_discovery=False)` forwards every call to the
  server. Example: `examples/mcp_read_resource.py`.

### Changed

- **BREAKING — a room holds one orchestration strategy** (RMK-665, RFC
  §19.7). `create_room(orchestration=...)` and a kit's default
  `orchestration` record the strategy they install, and `Loop`, `Pipeline`,
  `Supervisor` and `Swarm` check that record as they install: installing
  one of them by calling its `install(kit, room_id)` in a room created with
  another strategy raises `ValueError`, where both used to set up their
  hooks and tools side by side. Migration: call
  `kit.uninstall_strategy(room_id)` first, then
  `kit.install_strategy(room_id, strategy)`.
- **BREAKING — WhatsApp Personal's `reaction` event names its sender as a
  message does** (RMK-653): the `sender_id` an `on_event` callback receives
  is `+15551234567` where it was `15551234567`, and a sender behind a
  hidden-number id is their phone (`SenderAlt`) or the whole `<id>@lid`
  where it was the id's digits. Migration: compare it with a message's
  `sender_id` as it is; a callback that added the `+` itself drops that
  step.

### Fixed

- `LlamaCppAIProvider` starts `llama-server` with the host's own loader path
  when the host is a PyInstaller bundle. The bootloader points
  `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` (`DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH` on macOS) at the bundle and keeps
  the original as `<VAR>_ORIG`; the server inherited the bundle's path and
  could load the bundle's libstdc++, OpenSSL or libcurl instead of its own.
  The original value is restored, or only the bundle's entries removed when
  there was none, and the build's own library directories still come first.
  A host frozen by another tool keeps its environment as it is.
- A `RealtimeVoiceChannel` whose pipeline diarizes fires `ON_SPEAKER_CHANGE`,
  as a `VoiceChannel` does (RFC §12.3.9). The pipeline detected the changes
  but the realtime channel never subscribed to them, so diarization in
  speech-to-speech mode — one of its listed uses (RFC §12.4) — reached no
  hook. The hook carries `source="pipeline"`; a result attributing the audio
  to nobody is still no change.
- A `RealtimeVoiceChannel` whose pipeline runs at its own rate hands the
  provider audio at the provider's rate. Processed frames were resampled from
  the transport's rate, so a pipeline contract with a 16 kHz internal format
  (a diarization model's rate) in front of a 24 kHz transport and provider
  sent 16 kHz bytes as 24 kHz audio: the provider heard the user sped up, and
  nothing resampled at all when transport and provider rates matched. Frames
  are now resampled from their own rate, live and when held during the
  handshake; the inbound resampler is created when a frame first needs it.
- An `ACPChannel` opens a room's session once, whoever asks for it first
  (RMK-673). Two `set_config_option` calls during a standalone turn, or one
  racing the first prompt after it, each opened a session for the room, and
  the first one stayed open in the agent, unreachable. Openings now wait on a
  per-room lock of their own, a host call inside a turn included, and
  `close_session` waits for an opening in flight.
- `ACPChannel.cancel(room_id)` reaches a turn while its session is being
  opened (RMK-673): the agent starting, `session/new`, the session's setup.
  It returned `False` there, or sent `session/cancel` to a session not yet
  prompted, and the turn prompted anyway. The turn now ends without
  prompting, marked `interrupted`, and a standalone session it had opened is
  closed. `active_turns` counts such a turn as soon as it holds the room,
  where it counted it only once the prompt went out, so a caller retiring
  the channel no longer closes it under an opening turn.
- WhatsApp Personal answers a group in the group and names a hidden-number
  sender by their phone (RMK-653): a group message's room was found by its
  sender and answered them privately; the parser now names the group
  (`metadata["group_jid"]`) and `WhatsAppPersonalChannel` routes and answers
  by it, a private chat by the number (`TransportChannel` takes
  `reply_metadata_key` with `replies_to_sender`, the chat first). A sender
  WhatsApp hides behind an `@lid` id was kept as bare digits even when
  `SenderAlt` carried their phone, and E.164 made a wrong number of them
  (`+33123456789012345` with country code 33), answered at a wrong JID; the
  sender is now that phone, or the whole `<id>@lid`, never digits a
  normalizer reads (`roomkit.sources.neonize.sender_address`; a reaction's
  sender too, see Changed). neonize 0.5.2 addresses direct messages by LID,
  so these ids get commoner. A conversation met before under the old
  address opens a new room: a group's messages reach the group's room, not
  their sender's, and a hidden-number sender's reach the room of their phone
  or `<id>@lid`, not the one their digits opened. A custom `message_parser`
  sets `metadata["group_jid"]` to route a group the same way. `send_typing`
  and `mark_read` handed the source a JID object where it parses a string
  and failed on every call; a location went to a `send_location` neonize
  never had, and now goes out as a location message.
- `MCPToolProvider` reads every page of a server's `tools/list` (RMK-662, RFC
  §21.2): it read the first page and ignored `nextCursor`, so a server that
  pages its listing lost every tool after it. A server that pages on without
  bringing anything new (an empty page that still carries a cursor, a cursor
  handed out twice) or past 1000 pages ends the reading: a warning names the
  server and the provider keeps the tools read, where entering it would
  never have returned.
- An MCP tool call never lists the server's tools again (RMK-662, RFC §21.2).
  `MCPToolProvider` called through the SDK's `ClientSession.call_tool`, which
  sends a whole `tools/list` before every call of a tool its listing does not
